label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: National pharmacare after the Pharmacare Act: what was signed, what is covered, who is using it, and what full coverage would cost
citations: [20], [21], [22] are not on the Sources list (it has 19). Cite the number shown as "cite as [n]" in list_notes — not the note number.

review.sentence: Third, the coverage standard is specified in the statute rather than left to negotiation: universal, single-payer, first-dollar.
review.why: A peer-reviewed CMAJ analysis by Steven Morgan and Matthew Herder (the leading academic on Canadian pharmacare) finds that the Act "does not define what that means in terms of program design" and leaves the model to ministerial discretion in bilateral negotiations, permitting fill-the-gaps and different program structures across provinces. The section's stronger claim that the standard rules out deductibles and multi-payer models is contested by that reading.

review.sentence: The provinces that signed had to amend their own programs to meet that standard.
review.why: No note in the file says anything about provinces amending their own programs; the notes cover only the statutory text, royal assent, the planning duties and Health Canada's "learn by doing" page. The claim needs a source on the bilateral agreements or provincial legislation.

review.sentence: The same one-year window carries the other planning duties: a national bulk purchasing strategy, a pan-Canadian strategy on appropriate prescribing and use, and a committee of experts to advise on the implementation of national universal pharmacare [2].
review.why: The statute puts the committee of experts on a 30-day clock, not the one-year window: s.11(1) requires the Minister to establish it "no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent" (only its report is due within a year). The section's own note 39 records the 30-day requirement.

review.sentence: The Act itself does not use the phrase as a defined term in the provisions noted here; the two therapeutic categories in section 6(1) — contraception and diabetes — are the entire statutory scope of what the federal government may fund.
review.why: Section 5 commits the federal government to "maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples ... beginning with those for rare diseases", and the Minister's other obligations (ss. 7–11) contemplate a national formulary and universal pharmacare. Contraception and diabetes are the whole of the section 6(1) payment authority, not the whole of what the Act envisages funding.

review.sentence: These are the pieces that would matter if the program ever expanded past contraception and diabetes — a formulary defines what is in, a bulk purchasing strategy determines what is paid, and an appropriate-use strategy governs volume.
review.why: The section discusses the planning duties only in the future conditional, but Health Canada states all four statutory deliverables have already been completed and published (expert committee advice, CDA bulk-purchasing advice and essential drugs list, pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy), and only four provinces and territories have signed agreements. Both facts are material to judging what the Act has delivered.

review.sentence: The pharmacare agreement is more than $219 million over four years; it sits alongside a separate rare-disease agreement of over $48 million, for a combined $267 million [12].
review.why: The support checker gives about 17% that the passages noted from [12] state this.

review.sentence: The Act authorises contraception and diabetes only, so drugs for any other condition remain outside the program no matter how common or how costly.
review.why: The agreements themselves cover a third category: BC section 5.1 and Manitoba section 5.1 both commit to free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms for all residents — a non-contraception, non-diabetes therapy inside the program.

review.sentence: All four cover the insulins — fast-acting regular, lispro, aspart and glulisine; intermediate-acting isophane; the premixed human and lispro blends; and the long-acting glargine and detemir — along with metformin, glyburide and gliclazide, and the SGLT2 and DPP-4 combinations such as empagliflozin-metformin, dapagliflozin and the saxagliptin, linagliptin and sitagliptin families [7][8].
review.why: Two products are wrongly put in the common core: BC's Annex A lists glargine but no insulin detemir, and sitagliptin appears only in Manitoba's list (as sitagliptin and sitagliptin-metformin) — neither BC, PEI nor Yukon lists it.

review.sentence: For contraception, all four cover the combined oral contraceptives by active ingredient (levonorgestrel, desogestrel, drospirenone, norethindrone and norgestimate with ethinylestradiol), progestin-only pills, medroxyprogesterone, etonogestrel implants, both copper and progestogen IUDs, and the etonogestrel-ethinylestradiol vaginal ring [7][8].
review.why: Manitoba's Annex A entry for the vaginal ring is not a coverage commitment but "See note" — footnote 4 says only that Manitoba "will make best efforts to make this product (or an alternative) available over the course of the agreement."

review.sentence: In Manitoba, copper IUDs are provided "through public health programming" rather than through the pharmacy benefit, which means the device is free but the insertion pathway is not the same as walking into a pharmacy [8].
review.why: The agreement's condition column says only "Coverage provided through public health programming"; it does not say the device is free, and says nothing about insertion or pharmacy pathways — both are inferences added here.

review.sentence: The device stream, Stream 2, is the part of the program that expands access most unambiguously, because in most jurisdictions there was little or no prior public spending on the specific items.
review.why: Only BC's three device lines were $0. Manitoba reported $1,449,593 and Yukon $60,109, and PEI's $0 is expressly "beyond regular annual funding" for test strips and pumps, with its Stream 2 aimed partly at "lowering co-pay amounts" — so the money is not uniformly new coverage.

review.sentence: The SGLT2 inhibitors appear on the provincial lists; the GLP-1 agonists, including semaglutide, do not.
review.why: Manitoba's Annex A Table 1B lists "lixisenatide with insulin glargine" as an Exception Drug Status benefit — a GLP-1 receptor agonist is on at least one list, contradicting this absolute and the section's own earlier sentence.

review.sentence: People covered by a federal plan — the Non-Insured Health Benefits program for First Nations and Inuit, the Canadian Armed Forces, Veterans Affairs, Correctional Service Canada, the Interim Federal Health Program — keep that coverage rather than moving into pharmacare [6][7].
review.why: The support checker gives about 11% that the passages noted from [6] [7] state this.

review.sentence: Second, insulin and metformin are cheap relative to the drugs that are excluded: Health Canada puts insulin at $900 to $1,700 a year and metformin at about $100 [13].
review.why: The support checker gives about 19% that the passages noted from [13] state this.

sentences.sentence: Bill C-64 received royal assent on 10 October 2024 [2].

Section 6(1) obliges the minister to pay a province or territory only where an agreement has first been signed, and it confines what the money may be spent on: > "6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes." [2] Three things follow from that sentence, and each has consequences for how the program's delivery should be judged.

The Act does look past those two categories elsewhere: section 5 commits the federal government to "maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases" [2].

So the two categories are the whole of the payment authority, not the whole of what the statute contemplates funding — a distinction that matters when the rare-disease agreements are counted, since those exist with every province and territory [18].

Steven Morgan and Matthew Herder, in a peer-reviewed CMAJ analysis published before royal assent, argued that the phrase carries no operative definition: > "Bill C-64 refers to “universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage” but, unlike the _Canada Health Act_, it does not define what that means in terms of program design." [20] On their reading the Act "leaves that decision to the discretion of the federal health minister in bilateral negotiations with provinces and territories, and would permit different program structures across the country" [20].

Section 8(1) sets a one-year clock running from royal assent for the essential medicines list that is supposed to anchor a national formulary: > "8 (1) The Minister must, after discussions with the provinces and territories, request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare." [2] The same one-year window carries the other planning duties: a national bulk purchasing strategy and a pan-Canadian strategy on appropriate prescribing and use [2].

The committee of experts runs on a faster clock — the Act requires it be established within thirty days of royal assent, with its recommendations on the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare to follow [16].

Health Canada states that all four statutory deliverables have been completed: the committee of experts reported, the Canadian Drug Agency provided advice on a bulk purchasing strategy and an essential drugs list, and a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy was published [13].
The department's own framing of the sequencing is that the program will "learn by doing" [13].
As of Health Canada's own tracking page, the Government of Canada has signed pharmacare funding agreements with British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — and no one else [4].

The contrast with the adjacent file is stark: Canada has signed agreements with all provinces and territories under the National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases, a smaller program launched in the same period [18].
The four agreements share a template and even a title: "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" [4].

What differs is the money, the start date, and what the province already spent. **Manitoba** signed first, on 27 February 2025, and Health Canada calls it "the first-ever national pharmacare agreement" [11].
The pharmacare agreement is more than $219 million over four years; it sits alongside a separate rare-disease agreement of over $48 million, for a combined $267 million [12].
Stream 1 pays $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the following three years; Stream 2 is a one-time $9,945,348 in 2025-26 [8].

Manitoba's implementation date was 15 April 2025, and coverage of the majority of products was expected from June 2025 [8][12]. **British Columbia** signed second, on 6 March 2025, for "more than $670 million over four years" [11].

Stream 1 pays $17,406,567 in 2025-26 and then $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29 — a twelvefold jump between the first and second year — with Stream 2 a one-time $37,839,549 in 2026-27 [7].
That first-year figure is small because of the implementation date: BC's agreement sets it at 1 March 2026 [7].

British Columbia, which had run its own free-contraception program since April 2023, therefore went roughly a full year after signing with no federally funded first-dollar coverage in place, and the federal release told residents to expect coverage "in March 2026" [11]. **Prince Edward Island** signed on 7 March 2025.
Stream 1 pays $6,795,833 in 2025-26 and $7,404,416 in each of 2026-27 through 2028-29; Stream 2 is a one-time $1,188,243 [9].
Stream 1 pays nothing in 2025-26, then $2,548,410 in 2026-27 and $2,650,056 in each of 2027-28 and 2028-29; Stream 2 is a one-time $306,143 in 2025-26 [10].
Yukon's implementation date is the latest of the four: between 15 April and 5 May 2026 [10].
British Columbia spent $64,689,483 — $61,338,085 on diabetes and $3,351,398 on contraception [7].
Manitoba spent $23,945,982, of which only $750,746 was contraception [8].
Yukon spent $355,022, of which $1,467 was contraception [10].
Manitoba's 2022-23 spending on insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors was $1,449,593 [8].

BC's baseline for the three device categories it is expanding — hybrid closed-loop blood glucose monitor and insulin delivery systems, lancets for diabetic use, and additional supplies for insulin pump users — was $0 on all three [7].
PEI's device baseline was also $0 [9].
BC's obligation to report the savings delivered to residents on diabetes devices begins in fiscal year 2027-28, with the first report due 1 October 2027 [7].
The financial statements that would show how much federal money was actually spent on products, as opposed to administration and IT, also begin in 2027-28 [7].

The second is that both BC and Manitoba negotiated a benefit outside the federal streams: free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms, for all residents, effective 1 March 2026 in BC [7][8].

The funding is "subject to there being an appropriation of funds by the Parliament of Canada for the Fiscal Year in which any commitment would come due for payment", and Canada may reduce or terminate payments if authorities are amended or funding levels reduced, with 120 days' notice [7].
Pharmacare "covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications" and "only" covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee [5].
Two exclusions follow immediately in the same passage: delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees are not covered [5].
A person qualifies if they are a resident of a province or territory with an agreement in force and eligible for public health insurance there, with a valid prescription for a covered product [6].

Health Canada states the point that distinguishes this from every existing provincial drug program: "You're covered under pharmacare no matter your" age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [6].

Manitoba states it directly: "Clients with prescription medication coverage through a federal program are not eligible for coverage under MEPP." Those with 100 per cent coverage through the Non-Insured Health Benefits program or provincial employment and income assistance "are not eligible for MEPP and should continue to access their medications through these programs" [21].
BC's Plan NP is open to any resident enrolled in MSP, with exceptional coverage for those in the MSP wait period, but the same principle of not duplicating existing full coverage applies [22].

The core across the four includes the fast-acting insulins (regular, lispro, aspart and glulisine), intermediate-acting isophane, the premixed human and lispro blends, long-acting glargine, metformin, glyburide and gliclazide, and SGLT2 and DPP-4 combinations such as empagliflozin-metformin and dapagliflozin [7][8].

Outside that core the lists diverge in ways the announcements do not mention: insulin detemir appears on some provincial lists but not BC's, and sitagliptin and sitagliptin-metformin appear only on Manitoba's [7][8].

For contraception the common core is the combined oral contraceptives by active ingredient (levonorgestrel, desogestrel, drospirenone, norethindrone and norgestimate with ethinylestradiol), progestin-only pills, medroxyprogesterone, etonogestrel implants, copper and progestogen IUDs, and the etonogestrel-ethinylestradiol vaginal ring [7][8].

The ring is the exception that shows how thin the commitment can be: Manitoba's Annex A entry for it reads "See note", and the note says only that Manitoba "will make best efforts to make this product (or an alternative) available over the course of the agreement" [8].
Manitoba's list adds insulin degludec, glimepiride, acarbose, rosiglitazone, canagliflozin, repaglinide, glucagon and lixisenatide with insulin glargine [8].
BC's list does not carry all of those and instead specifies which brand-name versions are subject to its Low Cost Alternative policy [7].
Manitoba restricts a long list of its additions to Exception Drug Status, meaning the drug "is an eligible benefit only in Exception circumstances with prior approval from Manitoba" [8].

BC uses Special Authority for saxagliptin-metformin, linagliptin-metformin, pioglitazone, saxagliptin and linagliptin, and applies its Low Cost Alternative policy to brand-name metformin, gliclazide, dapagliflozin and several contraceptives, so that residents may be responsible for paying a portion of costs for the brand product where a cheaper generic is available free [7].

In practice BC removed most prior-approval requirements at launch — empagliflozin, empagliflozin-metformin, gliclazide, insulin glargine and topical estrogen no longer need Special Authority, and "No MHTs or contraceptives will require SA" [22].
Where a product is fully covered, BC's protection is strong: the Full Payment Policy means "pharmacies cannot charge a client for the medication or any service associated with the dispense" [22].

It covers the cost of the product up to the lowest-cost interchangeable option plus "a professional fee of up to $14," but limits that fee to once a month for diabetes and HIV medications and once every three months for oral contraceptives, and states that any additional fees a pharmacy chooses to charge will not be covered [21].
Manitoba covers levonorgestrel emergency contraception to "Maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year" [8].

In Manitoba, copper IUDs are handled outside the pharmacy benefit altogether: the province lists them as available "at no cost directly from your health care provider", and states that "Copper IUDs dispensed through community pharmacies are not covered under MEPP" [21].
A Manitoban who fills a copper IUD prescription at a pharmacy pays for it and cannot be reimbursed [21].
BC covers copper and progestogen IUDs as regular benefits, with the brand-name vaginal ring subject to the Low Cost Alternative policy [7].

BC's Stream 2 objectives are to "support hybrid closed-loop blood glucose monitor and insulin delivery systems; to include lancets for diabetic use; and to include additional supplies for insulin pump and glucose monitor users" [7], and BC's 2022-23 spending on all three categories was $0 [7].

What that money bought is now documented: from 1 April 2026 BC expanded coverage of alcohol wipes, lancets and blood and urine ketone strips, and it listed the mylife Ypsopump on 17 December 2025 and the Omnipod 5 hybrid closed-loop automated insulin delivery system on 1 April 2026, with the expansion attributed to federal pharmacare funding [22].
Manitoba's Stream 2 targets insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors, on which it already spent $1,449,593 in 2022-23 [8].
PEI's device baseline was $0, but its Stream 2 is aimed partly at lowering co-pay amounts rather than adding categories [9].

Manitoba is the clearest case: its Enhanced Pharmacare Program covers four categories — birth control, diabetes, HIV prevention and treatment, and hormone replacement therapy — and states that federal funding supports only the diabetes and birth control portions [21].
PrEP, PEP and antiretroviral therapy are free in Manitoba under a provincial decision the Pharmacare Act does not fund [21].
BC created a parallel Plan NP covering diabetes medications, menopausal hormone therapy and contraceptives, with the MHT benefit added by the province [22].
Manitoba answers the question directly: "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories" [21].

CIHI measured spending on GLP-1 analogues and SGLT2 inhibitors at $868 million in 2022, representing 24% of total growth in public drug program spending, with Ozempic alone rising from $265 million in 2021 to $434 million in 2022 [17].

The SGLT2 inhibitors are on the provincial lists; the GLP-1 agonists largely are not, with the narrow exception of lixisenatide with insulin glargine on Manitoba's list as an Exception Drug Status benefit [8].
On cost per patient, Health Canada's own framing gives the scale: insulin runs $900 to $1,700 a year and metformin about $100 [13].

About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes, and costs to the health care system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion in 2018, projected to surpass $39 billion by 2028 [13].

At royal assent, Health Canada said the agreements would give "up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada free access to contraception" and that "the 3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes will have universal access to a suite of medications" [16].

For individual deals the same construction recurs: the Manitoba agreement "will support the reproductive freedom of nearly 350,000 Manitobans" and ensure "over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes can access essential medications" [12]; the BC deal was announced as covering more than 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 people with diabetes [11].

Prince Edward Island's earlier federal-funded program, the $5 copay initiative launched in June 2023, generated a measurable result: PEI residents "saved over $2 million in out-of-pocket costs on more than 230,000 prescriptions" under the program, and the copay reduction applied to almost 60% of medications regularly used by Island residents [16].
"In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception," and since the program began "more than 306,000 people have benefitted" [11].
BC's obligation to report the savings delivered to residents on diabetes devices begins in fiscal year 2027-28, with the first report due 1 October 2027 [7].
The attested financial statements — which would show how much federal money was spent on products as distinct from administration, IT and evaluation — also begin in 2027-28 [7].

The agreements require provinces to publish which products are covered and how to access them, and to report their 2022-23 baseline spending, but not to report prescription volumes, beneficiary counts or out-of-pocket savings in the first two years of operation [7][8].
Manitoba's agreement requires it to publish the covered products by its implementation date and to report how Stream 2 money was used, but again no utilization data [8].
Two of the four implementation dates fell in 2025 — Manitoba on 15 April and PEI on 1 May — while the other two fall in 2026, BC on 1 March and Yukon between 15 April and 5 May [7][8][9][10].

Getting them straight resolves most of the apparent disagreement with other estimates. **The headline public-sector cost.** PBO estimates "the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28" [15].

PBO states: "As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs." [15] Any statement that the PBO put a federal price tag on pharmacare — $11.2 billion, $13.4 billion, or any other — misreads the report.

The federal share depends on a cost-sharing formula that no government has settled. **The gross cost to public drug plans.** PBO estimates "the gross cost incremental to that of public drug plans will be $14.8 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $17.3 billion in 2027-28" [15].

It is the number to use when the question is what the program spends on drugs, before asking who pays and what it displaces. **The economy-wide result.** Total drug expenditure under Pharmacare would be $33.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28, but against the status quo PBO finds economy-wide savings of $1.4 billion rising to $2.2 billion, because Pharmacare spending grows at 5.3% a year against 5.8% under the baseline [15].

The benefit design is universal and replaces existing public and private plans, using the RAMQ formulary as the national formulary, with "a $5 co-payment for all prescriptions of brand-name drugs" and exemptions for under-16s, students aged 16 to 18, people over 65, pregnant women, the physically disabled, and employment insurance and social assistance recipients [15].

The central behavioural assumption is stated in the report: "Prices borne directly by patients are expected to fall by 47 per cent to 100 per cent, which results in overall increases in the utilization of prescription drugs of 13.5 per cent." [15] That 13.5% is doing a lot of work.

Under a catastrophic formulary — one that covers only very high drug costs — "the incremental cost of a single-payer universal drug plan with a catastrophic formulary to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $1.8 billion and $2.0 billion in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [15].

Under an essential-medicines formulary, the result is startling in the other direction: PBO estimates drug expenditures "to be $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than the estimated spending under the baseline scenario in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [15].

The GLP-1 class illustrates the exposure: CIHI measured spending on GLP-1 analogues and SGLT2 inhibitors at $868 million in 2022, representing 24% of total growth in public drug program spending, with Ozempic alone rising from $265 million to $434 million in a year [17].

Its central estimate was incremental and staged: > "We have estimated that it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines." [1] The same report projected the cost of a comprehensive formulary rather than an essential-medicines one at $15.3 billion by 2027 [1].

The most influential Canadian model, Morgan and colleagues in CMAJ in 2015, found that total spending would fall: > "Universal public drug coverage would reduce total spending on prescription drugs in Canada by $7.3 billion (worst-case scenario $4.2 billion, best-case scenario $9.4 billion)." [3] That is a 32% reduction in total Canadian prescription spending in the central case, and the paper's striking result is on the government side: a net government cost of roughly $958 million, because universal public coverage replaces existing public spending, private insurance premiums and out-of-pocket payments rather than adding a new layer on top [3].

notes.claim: The Hoskins advisory council (2019) estimated incremental costs of $3.5B in 2022 for an essential-medicines start, rising to $15.3B in 2027 for a comprehensive formulary.

| **Total**                               | **$3,463,296**          |
notes.claim: PEI's federal money exceeds its entire prior-year spend on the same products more than twice over: $6.8M federal in 2025-26 against a $3.46M 2022-23 baseline, and its Stream 2 diabetes device baseline was $0.

notes.quote:
| Contraception                           | $1,467           |
| Diabetes                                | $353,555         |
| **Total**                               | **$355,022**     |
notes.claim: Yukon's 2022-23 baseline public spending was $355,022 on the Annex A drugs ($1,467 contraception, $353,555 diabetes) and $60,109 on insulin pumps and glucose monitors — so the federal Stream 1 money of $2.5M+ is several times its prior spend.

notes.quote: announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC.
notes.claim: BC deal headline: more than $670 million over four years, framed as covering over 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 people with diabetes. BC residents were told to expect coverage to begin in March 2026.

notes.quote: On February 27, 2025, the Government of Canada announced the first-ever national pharmacare agreement with Manitoba providing more than $219 million over four years to improve access to contraceptives, diabetes medications and diabetes devices and supplies for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Health Canada's own release states Manitoba's was "the first-ever national pharmacare agreement" at more than $219 million over four years, signed 27 February 2025 — so BC, despite the earlier provincial contraception program, was second to sign.

notes.quote: On April 1, 2023, the province began providing free contraceptives to all residents. In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted.
notes.claim: BC's own free-contraception program, running since 1 April 2023 and therefore independent of the federal deal, served approximately 227,000 people in 2024 alone and more than 306,000 since launch — the clearest real uptake figure available for a contraception benefit in Canada.

notes.quote: Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Manitoba deal: $267M total federal investment across two bilateral agreements, of which more than $219M over four years is the pharmacare agreement; the rest, over $48M, is for rare diseases. Manitoba coverage was expected for the majority of products from June 2025.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of nearly 350,000 Manitobans and make sure that over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes can access essential medications to reduce their risk of serious health complications and improve their quality of life.
notes.claim: Health Canada's population reach figures for Manitoba: nearly 350,000 people for contraception and over 149,000 with diabetes.

notes.quote: As set out in the act, we have:
notes.claim: Health Canada confirms all four statutory planning deliverables were completed: expert committee advice, CDA advice on a bulk purchasing strategy and an essential drugs list, and a published pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy. The stated approach is "learn by doing".

notes.quote: About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes. In 2018, costs to the healthcare system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion, and they could surpass $39 billion by 2028.
notes.claim: Scale of the diabetes benefit: about 3.8 million people in Canada diagnosed with diabetes; 2018 health system costs estimated at $27 billion, projected to exceed $39 billion by 2028. Insulin costs $900-$1,700 a year, metformin about $100.

notes.quote: The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2).
notes.claim: The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts (2025) estimated the total cost of publicly funding an essential medicines list at between $6 and $10 billion, and proposed the federal government pay the entire cost.

notes.quote: Source : Source : Committee estimations using data from IQVIA Solutions Canada, the Canadian Institute for Health Information and reports from the Parliamentary Budget Officer
notes.claim: The committee's 2025 spending comparison: status quo out-of-pocket $9.5B, private insurance $17.3B, public plans $18.8B; under pharmacare out-of-pocket falls to $6.8B, private to $12.5B, public plans to $13.6B, with a new pharmacare line of $8B — so total system spending falls.

notes.quote: Total spending on prescribed drugs in Canada jumped by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024
notes.claim: Total Canadian spending on prescribed drugs rose from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024 — a $10 billion increase in five years with, the committee says, no measurable improvement in health or access.

notes.quote: The cost of pharmacare in 2025 to 26 is projected to be between $6.0 and $9.8 billion.
notes.claim: The committee's own bottom line: the cost of pharmacare in 2025-26 is projected at between $6.0 and $9.8 billion, and it stresses the range is design-dependent — lower with fewer medicines or bigger price cuts, higher with a longer list or current prices.

notes.quote: we estimate the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.
notes.claim: PBO's headline: under a single-payer universal plan based on Quebec's RAMQ formulary, the incremental cost to the public sector (federal and provincial combined) is $11.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.

notes.quote: As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs.
notes.claim: PBO states explicitly that it cannot isolate the federal share: because no federal-provincial cost-sharing model has been settled, only the combined public-sector cost is estimable.

notes.quote: PBO estimates the gross cost incremental to that of public drug plans will be $14.8 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $17.3 billion in 2027-28.
notes.claim: PBO's gross figure and economy-wide result: total drug expenditure under Pharmacare $33.2B in 2024-25 rising to $38.9B in 2027-28; gross cost incremental to public drug plans $14.8B rising to $17.3B; but economy-wide savings of $1.4B rising to $2.2B, because Pharmacare spending grows at 5.3% versus 5.8% baseline.

notes.quote: Once copayment revenues and savings on direct federal spending are accounted for, the incremental cost of a single-payer universal drug plan with a catastrophic formulary to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $1.8 billion and $2.0 billion in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively.
notes.claim: PBO's alternative-formulary results are the most useful comparison for the current first phase: a catastrophic formulary costs the public sector $1.8B in 2024-25 and $2.0B in 2027-28, while an essential-medicines formulary actually costs $0.4B and $0.3B more than the status quo baseline because its generic drugs are already cheap and the added utilization is not offset by savings.

notes.quote: Prices borne directly by patients are expected to fall by 47 per cent to 100 per cent, which results in overall increases in the utilization of prescription drugs of 13.5 per cent.
notes.claim: PBO's key behavioural assumption: prices borne by patients fall 47% to 100%, producing a 13.5% increase in prescription utilization — the mechanism by which universal coverage raises volume.

notes.quote: Require a $5 co-payment for all prescriptions of brand-name drugs, with exemptions for the following:
notes.claim: PBO's benefit design: universal, replacing existing public and private plans, RAMQ formulary as national formulary, with a $5 brand-name copayment and exemptions for under-16s, students 16-18, over-65s, pregnant women, the physically disabled, EI and social assistance recipients.

notes.quote: PBO estimates that drug expenditures under this alternative to be $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than the estimated spending under the baseline scenario in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively.
notes.claim: Under the essential-medicines formulary, PBO finds drug expenditures come in $0.4B (2024-25) and $0.3B (2027-28) above the baseline, because the list is mostly generics already priced low, so stronger purchasing adds little saving against added use.

notes.quote: These agreements will support reproductive freedom by providing up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada free access to contraception. Additionally, the 3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes will have universal access to a suite of medications that reduce the risk of serious health complications and improve quality of life.
notes.claim: The stated scale of the intended first phase at royal assent: up to nine million women and gender-diverse people for contraception and 3.7 million people with diabetes for medications — the government's own denominator for judging uptake.

notes.quote: The Act also requires that a committee of experts be established within thirty days to make recommendations on the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare in Canada.
notes.claim: The Act required a committee of experts be established within 30 days to recommend on operation and financing, and created a fund for diabetes devices and supplies — the statutory basis for Stream 2.

notes.quote: Public drug program spending in Canada was $17.2 billion in 2022.
notes.claim: CIHI's measured baseline: public drug program spending in Canada was $17.2 billion in 2022, up 6.4% from 2021, with 43.3% of that spending going to the 2.2% of beneficiaries for whom a program paid $10,000 or more.

notes.quote: Spending on glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) analogues and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors reached $868 million, representing 24% of total growth in public drug program spending.
notes.claim: CIHI measured spending on GLP-1 analogues and SGLT2 inhibitors at $868 million in 2022, 24% of total public drug program spending growth, with Ozempic alone rising from $265M to $434M — the drug class driving growth fastest.

notes.quote: It won't cover any applicable:
notes.claim: Coverage limits stated plainly: pharmacare pays listed products plus the dispensing fee, but not delivery fees or pharmacist prescribing fees — a first-dollar benefit that is not quite zero-cost at the counter for some access routes.

notes.quote: Exception Drug Status (EDS) benefit: the drug or related product is an eligible benefit only in Exception circumstances with prior approval from Manitoba.
notes.claim: The Manitoba formulary is broader than PEI's and Yukon's: it adds degludec, glimepiride, acarbose, rosiglitazone, canagliflozin, repaglinide and several SGLT2/DPP-4 combinations, many restricted to Exception Drug Status with prior approval — so "free" varies by product even within one province.

notes.claim: Manitoba caps one contraceptive product: levonorgestrel emergency contraception is limited to a maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year, and copper IUDs are delivered through public health programming rather than the pharmacy benefit.
BC's 2022-23 public spending on the Annex A products was $64,689,483 ($61.3M diabetes, $3.35M contraception), against which its ~$205M annual federal Stream 1 transfer is roughly triple.

notes.claim: Critical for the uptake question: BC's results reporting obligation on diabetes device savings does not begin until Fiscal Year 2027-28, with the first report due 1 October 2027 — so the agreements themselves build in no public results data before then.
