notes.claim: Manitoba's Stream 2 device baseline was $1,449,593 for insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors, and BC's baseline for the devices it is expanding (hybrid closed-loop systems, lancets, pump supplies) was $0 — the device money is genuinely new spending.

notes.quote: Effective on March 1, 2026, British Columbia will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: BC's agreement adds free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms effective 1 March 2026 — a provincial add-on alongside the federal deal, as Manitoba did.

notes.quote: Manitoba will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies specified by Manitoba to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: Manitoba's agreement likewise commits to free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms for all residents — the same add-on negotiated in both provinces.

notes.quote: Canada has also signed agreements with all provinces and territories in support of the first-ever National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases.
notes.claim: The contrast that frames the delivery record: Canada has signed rare-disease agreements with all provinces and territories, while pharmacare agreements exist with only "a number" — four. Federal plans cover about 1 million people directly.

notes.quote: Estimated savings from universal public coverage of these essential medicines was $4.27 billion per year (range $2.72 billion to $5.83 billion; 28% reduction) for patients and private drug plan sponsors, at an incremental government cost of $1.23 billion per year (range $373 million to $1.98 billion; 11% reduction).
notes.claim: The 2017 essential-medicines model: incremental government cost $1.23 billion a year (range $373M-$1.98B) while patients and private plan sponsors saved $4.27 billion a year (range $2.72B-$5.83B, a 28% reduction) — total spending would fall $3.04 billion.

notes.quote: Patients finance 22% of total Canadian prescription drug expenditures out of pocket.4
notes.claim: Morgan et al. state the pre-existing baseline explicitly: patients paid 22% of total Canadian prescription drug expenditures out of pocket, private plans 35%, provincial plans 25% to 41% by jurisdiction, and the federal government covered select populations accounting for 2% of expenditure.

notes.quote: The estimated gross cost to governments (excluding indirect savings on public sector employee benefits) is $1.2 billion for coverage of essential medicines in 2015, as compared with the estimated $3.4 billion for comprehensive public drug coverage in 2012/13.
notes.claim: The direct comparison of the two Morgan models in the same paper: $1.2 billion gross cost for essential medicines coverage in 2015 versus $3.4 billion estimated for comprehensive public drug coverage in 2012/13 — benefit design, not method, drives the gap.

notes.quote: Since then, PEI residents have saved over $2 million in out-of-pocket costs on more than 230,000 prescriptions under PEI’s $5 copay program, which was launched in June 2023 and reduced copays for almost 60% of medications regularly used by Island residents.
notes.claim: PEI's earlier federal-funded $5 copay program (launched June 2023) generated a measurable uptake figure: residents saved over $2 million in out-of-pocket costs on more than 230,000 prescriptions, and the copay reduction covered almost 60% of medications regularly used by Island residents.

notes.quote: announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC.
notes.claim: BC's deal was framed as reaching over 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 people with diabetes — projected reach, not measured use.

notes.quote: Effective on March 1, 2026, British Columbia will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: The agreements themselves cover a therapy that is neither contraception nor diabetes: BC (section 5.1) and Manitoba (section 5.1, "Manitoba will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies specified by Manitoba to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents") both add free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy. So it is not true that drugs for any other condition remain outside the program.

notes.quote: As written, the bill leaves that decision to the discretion of the federal health minister in bilateral negotiations with provinces and territories, and would permit different program structures across the country.
notes.claim: The same CMAJ analysis says the coverage model is left to ministerial discretion in bilateral negotiations, not fixed by the statute.

notes.quote: 11 (1) The Minister must, no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent, establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare.
notes.claim: The committee of experts had a 30-day establishment deadline (with a one-year report deadline), not the one-year planning window the section groups it under.

notes.quote: 5 The Government of Canada commits to maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases.
notes.claim: Section 5 commits long-term federal funding beyond contraception and diabetes, beginning with rare-disease drugs, so section 6(1)'s two categories are not the whole of what the Act contemplates funding.

notes.quote: As set out in the act, we have:
notes.claim: Health Canada states that all the statutory planning deliverables (expert committee advice, CDA advice on bulk purchasing and the essential drugs list, and a published appropriate-use strategy) have been completed — so the planning duties are past deliverables, not only future ones.

notes.quote: does not define what that means in terms of program design
notes.claim: Peer-reviewed CMAJ analysis (Morgan and Herder) argues the Act's "universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage" wording is undefined in program-design terms, so the statute does not fix a coverage model or rule out fill-the-gaps/multi-payer approaches.

notes.quote: The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2).
notes.claim: The 2025 National Pharmacare Committee of Experts — the most recent official Canadian estimate — puts publicly funding an essential medicines list at $6-10 billion, roughly double the Hoskins council's $3.5B launch figure for a comparable benefit design.

notes.quote: Public drug program spending in Canada was $17.2 billion in 2022.
notes.claim: CIHI's measured baseline for public drug program spending ($17.2B in 2022, up 6.4%) is available and was already noted for this section, contradicting the section's statement that the CIHI total has not been established.

notes.quote: As early as 2022, when national pharmacare would cover essential medications, total spending on prescription drugs would be $300 million lower than without pharmacare.
notes.claim: At launch (2022), the Hoskins council projected total system spending only $300 million lower than the status quo — so purchasing savings did not offset a substantial part of the $7.6B gross cost in the launch year; the gap between gross and incremental is mostly displaced existing public spending.

notes.quote: As written, the bill leaves that decision to the discretion of the federal health minister in bilateral negotiations with provinces and territories, and would permit different program structures across the country.
notes.claim: Morgan and Herder conclude the Act as written creates a fill-the-gaps system rather than universal public pharmacare, and that the decision is left to the federal health minister's discretion in bilateral negotiations.

notes.quote: According to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, 43% of the cost of the fill-the-gaps pharmacare plan that Bill C-64 would create as written will be financed through private insurance plans.
notes.claim: Morgan and Herder cite a PBO costing of Bill C-64 itself finding that 43% of the cost of the fill-the-gaps plan the Act would create would be financed through private insurance plans — a distinct PBO publication from the single-payer costing.

notes.quote: In contrast to the fill-the-gaps approach to covering these medicines, this universal, public approach would save provincial governments $1.3 billion over the first 5 years and reduce total program costs by $1.1 billion over that period, through bulk purchasing and administrative efficiencies.
notes.claim: Morgan and Herder estimate that a universal public approach to the first phase — federal procurement and no-cost distribution to provinces, as with COVID-19 vaccines — would save provincial governments $1.3 billion over five years and cut total program costs by $1.1 billion.

notes.quote: Bill C-64 refers to “universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage” but, unlike the _Canada Health Act_, it does not define what that means in terms of program design.
notes.claim: Morgan and Herder's peer-reviewed CMAJ analysis argues the Act's phrase "universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage" is left undefined, unlike the Canada Health Act, so the program design is settled by ministerial discretion rather than statute.

notes.quote: Effective April 15, 2025, the Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program (MEPP) provides eligible Manitoba residents with no cost coverage of most medications for:
notes.claim: Manitoba's Enhanced Pharmacare Program covers four categories, not two: birth control, diabetes, HIV prevention and treatment, and hormone replacement therapy. Federal funding supports only the diabetes and birth control portions — the HIV and HRT benefits are provincial additions.

notes.quote: Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories.
notes.claim: Manitoba states plainly why semaglutide is excluded from free coverage: Ozempic was not on the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage negotiated with provinces — confirming the GLP-1 exclusion is a federal formulary decision, not a provincial one.

notes.quote: Most medications used for the prevention and treatment of HIV are covered under MEPP. This includes:
notes.claim: Manitoba confirms HIV prevention and treatment is inside its free program: PrEP, PEP and antiretroviral therapy are all covered at no cost under MEPP — a benefit category the federal Pharmacare Act does not fund.

notes.quote: MEPP covers the cost of eligible products (up to the lowest cost interchangeable product) and a professional fee of up to $14.
notes.claim: Manitoba's MEPP caps the professional fee at $14 and limits it to once a month for diabetes/HIV drugs and once every three months for oral contraceptives; emergency contraceptive pills are covered up to three times per fiscal year. Pharmacy fees above these are not covered.

notes.quote: As of March 1, 2026, the National Pharmacare Plan (Plan NP) provides 100% coverage of select diabetes medications, menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), and contraceptives for any B.C. resident enrolled in MSP.
notes.claim: BC's Plan NP is live: from 1 March 2026 it provides 100% coverage of select diabetes medications, menopausal hormone therapy and contraceptives for any BC resident enrolled in MSP, with federal funding contributing. The Full Payment Policy means pharmacies cannot charge the client for the medication or any associated service.

notes.quote: On April 1, 2026, BC PharmaCare expanded coverage of certain diabetes-related devices and supplies, made possible by federal national pharmacare funding.
notes.claim: BC used federal device money to expand coverage of alcohol wipes, lancets and blood/urine ketone strips from 1 April 2026, and listed the mylife Ypsopump (17 December 2025) and the Omnipod 5 hybrid closed-loop system (1 April 2026) — concrete evidence of what Stream 2 bought.

notes.quote: No MHTs or contraceptives will require SA.
notes.claim: BC confirms most Special Authority requirements were removed at launch: empagliflozin, empagliflozin/metformin, gliclazide, insulin glargine and topical estrogen no longer need pre-approval, and no MHT or contraceptives require it — but saxagliptin, linagliptin and pioglitazone still do.

notes.quote: As of March 1, 2026, the same contraceptives previously covered under Plan Z are now covered under the National Pharmacare Plan (Plan NP).
notes.claim: BC confirms the shift of coverage from Plan Z to Plan NP on 1 March 2026 — the contraceptives BC already funded provincially were relabelled into the federally funded plan, which is the substitution mechanism in action.

report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act actually commits Canada to: royal assent, the statutory tests provinces must meet, the money attached, and how a "first phase" was defined

The Pharmacare Act is a short statute with a long shadow, and the gap between what it says and what people assume it says explains most of the confusion in the current debate. Bill C-64 received royal assent on 10 October 2024 [2]. It did not create a national pharmacare program. It created a conditional spending power: a legal authority for the federal health minister to send money to provinces and territories that sign agreements, plus a list of planning obligations with deadlines attached.

The payment provision is the heart of it, and its grammar matters. Section 6(1) obliges the minister to pay a province or territory only where an agreement has first been signed, and it confines what the money may be spent on:

> "6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes." [2]

Three things follow from that sentence, and each has consequences for how the program's delivery should be judged. First, the federal obligation is triggered by provincial consent, not by citizenship: a resident of a province that has not signed is not owed anything under the Act, and no payment flows. Second, the statutory purpose of the payment is narrower than "pharmacare" as that word is normally used. Section 6(1) authorises coverage for contraception and for the treatment of diabetes, not for prescription drugs in general. Any claim that the Act delivered universal drug coverage is a claim about a program this provision does not describe. The Act does look past those two categories elsewhere: section 5 commits the federal government to "maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases" [2]. So the two categories are the whole of the payment authority, not the whole of what the statute contemplates funding — a distinction that matters when the rare-disease agreements are counted, since those exist with every province and territory [18]. Third, the Act names a coverage standard — universal, single-payer, first-dollar — but does not define it.

That third point is contested, and the contest matters. Steven Morgan and Matthew Herder, in a peer-reviewed CMAJ analysis published before royal assent, argued that the phrase carries no operative definition:

> "Bill C-64 refers to “universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage” but, unlike the _Canada Health Act_, it does not define what that means in terms of program design." [20]

On their reading the Act "leaves that decision to the discretion of the federal health minister in bilateral negotiations with provinces and territories, and would permit different program structures across the country" [20]. That is a stronger claim than reading the words as self-executing, and it has been borne out in practice: the four agreements signed so far deliver coverage through four different provincial vehicles — BC's Plan NP, Manitoba's Enhanced Pharmacare Program, and the PEI and Yukon equivalents — each with its own formulary, its own prior-approval rules and its own fee caps. Morgan and Herder's conclusion that the Act creates a fill-the-gaps system rather than a public one is a policy judgement, not a finding of fact, but their textual point is correct: the Canada Health Act defines its criteria and attaches consequences to them, and this Act does neither.

The Act's substantive obligations are procedural and deadline-bound rather than financial. Section 8(1) sets a one-year clock running from royal assent for the essential medicines list that is supposed to anchor a national formulary:

> "8 (1) The Minister must, after discussions with the provinces and territories, request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare." [2]

The same one-year window carries the other planning duties: a national bulk purchasing strategy and a pan-Canadian strategy on appropriate prescribing and use [2]. The committee of experts runs on a faster clock — the Act requires it be established within thirty days of royal assent, with its recommendations on the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare to follow [16].

These are the pieces that would matter if the program ever expanded past contraception and diabetes — a formulary defines what is in, a bulk purchasing strategy determines what is paid, and an appropriate-use strategy governs volume. None of them delivers a covered prescription on its own. What is notable, and under-reported, is that the planning work is further along than the delivery. Health Canada states that all four statutory deliverables have been completed: the committee of experts reported, the Canadian Drug Agency provided advice on a bulk purchasing strategy and an essential drugs list, and a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy was published [13]. The department's own framing of the sequencing is that the program will "learn by doing" [13]. Four provinces and territories have signed agreements; the planning architecture exists on paper and in advice, while the benefit reaches a minority of the country.

That structure is why the honest answer to "what has pharmacare delivered" has to be assembled from provincial agreements and administrative data rather than read off the statute. The Act supplies the terms, the standard of coverage and the deadline for the planning work; it supplies no drugs. Everything concrete — which provinces are in, which products are listed, how many people have filled a prescription — lives in the bilateral agreements and in the federal and provincial reporting that follows them. The remainder of this report takes those in turn.

One clarification is needed on the word "first phase," which is used loosely in press coverage and precisely nowhere in the section quoted above. The Act itself does not use the phrase as a defined term in the provisions noted here; the two therapeutic categories in section 6(1) — contraception and diabetes — are the entire statutory scope of what the federal government may fund. When ministers describe the program as a "first phase" toward comprehensive coverage, they are describing an intention, not a statutory commitment. The Act's planning obligations point toward a national formulary and universal pharmacare, but nothing in the payment provision requires a future government to add a third category of drug, and the money for any expansion would have to be appropriated again. This distinction — a first phase by design versus a first phase by aspiration — is the single most important thing to hold onto when assessing the cost estimates discussed later, because those estimates price a comprehensive program that no statute currently obliges anyone to build.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements, in what order, for how much, and which have not — including the territories' separate arrangements

Four. That is the whole list. As of Health Canada's own tracking page, the Government of Canada has signed pharmacare funding agreements with British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — and no one else [4]. Nine provinces and territories, containing the large majority of Canada's population, have no pharmacare agreement: Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Northwest Territories and Nunavut. The contrast with the adjacent file is stark: Canada has signed agreements with all provinces and territories under the National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases, a smaller program launched in the same period [18].

The four agreements share a template and even a title: "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" [4]. Each has two funding streams — Stream 1 for the drug benefit itself, Stream 2 a one-time payment for diabetes devices and supplies — and each runs to 31 March 2029. What differs is the money, the start date, and what the province already spent.

**Manitoba** signed first, on 27 February 2025, and Health Canada calls it "the first-ever national pharmacare agreement" [11]. The pharmacare agreement is more than $219 million over four years; it sits alongside a separate rare-disease agreement of over $48 million, for a combined $267 million [12]. Stream 1 pays $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the following three years; Stream 2 is a one-time $9,945,348 in 2025-26 [8]. Manitoba's implementation date was 15 April 2025, and coverage of the majority of products was expected from June 2025 [8][12].

**British Columbia** signed second, on 6 March 2025, for "more than $670 million over four years" [11]. Stream 1 pays $17,406,567 in 2025-26 and then $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29 — a twelvefold jump between the first and second year — with Stream 2 a one-time $37,839,549 in 2026-27 [7]. That first-year figure is small because of the implementation date: BC's agreement sets it at 1 March 2026 [7]. British Columbia, which had run its own free-contraception program since April 2023, therefore went roughly a full year after signing with no federally funded first-dollar coverage in place, and the federal release told residents to expect coverage "in March 2026" [11].

**Prince Edward Island** signed on 7 March 2025. Stream 1 pays $6,795,833 in 2025-26 and $7,404,416 in each of 2026-27 through 2028-29; Stream 2 is a one-time $1,188,243 [9]. PEI's implementation date was 1 May 2025.

**Yukon** signed on 20 March 2025. Stream 1 pays nothing in 2025-26, then $2,548,410 in 2026-27 and $2,650,056 in each of 2027-28 and 2028-29; Stream 2 is a one-time $306,143 in 2025-26 [10]. Yukon's implementation date is the latest of the four: between 15 April and 5 May 2026 [10].

The baseline spending figures in Annex B of each agreement are the most revealing numbers in the whole file, because they show what each province was already paying for the same products in 2022-23 before any federal money arrived. British Columbia spent $64,689,483 — $61,338,085 on diabetes and $3,351,398 on contraception [7]. Manitoba spent $23,945,982, of which only $750,746 was contraception [8]. PEI spent $3,463,296 [9]. Yukon spent $355,022, of which $1,467 was contraception [10].

Set those against the federal transfers and a pattern appears that is not obvious from the headline announcements. BC's roughly $205 million annual Stream 1 transfer is about three times its own prior spending on the same products. PEI's $6,795,833 first-year transfer is roughly double its $3,463,296 baseline. Yukon's $2,548,410 in 2026-27 is more than seven times its $355,022 baseline. Manitoba is the outlier: its $54,603,615 annual transfer is about 2.3 times its $23,945,982 baseline, and its contraceptive spending was so low ($750,746) that near-universal coverage is a genuine expansion rather than a top-up. This is my inference from the annex figures rather than a claim any of the agreements make, but the arithmetic suggests the federal money is doing two different jobs at once — funding a real coverage expansion in the small jurisdictions, and in BC substantially displacing provincial spending on a benefit the province had already chosen to fund itself.

The device money is cleaner, because most of it is new. Manitoba's 2022-23 spending on insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors was $1,449,593 [8]. BC's baseline for the three device categories it is expanding — hybrid closed-loop blood glucose monitor and insulin delivery systems, lancets for diabetic use, and additional supplies for insulin pump users — was $0 on all three [7]. PEI's device baseline was also $0 [9]. The Stream 2 payments are therefore the part of the program that most clearly adds coverage rather than substituting for it.

Two features of the agreements bear on whether the program can be evaluated at all. The first is that results reporting is deferred. BC's obligation to report the savings delivered to residents on diabetes devices begins in fiscal year 2027-28, with the first report due 1 October 2027 [7]. The financial statements that would show how much federal money was actually spent on products, as opposed to administration and IT, also begin in 2027-28 [7]. Nothing in the agreements requires public reporting of prescription volumes or beneficiary counts in the first two years of operation. The second is that both BC and Manitoba negotiated a benefit outside the federal streams: free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms, for all residents, effective 1 March 2026 in BC [7][8]. That is a provincial addition, not federal pharmacare, and it should not be counted as part of what the Pharmacare Act delivered.

There is also a fiscal caveat written into every agreement. The funding is "subject to there being an appropriation of funds by the Parliament of Canada for the Fiscal Year in which any commitment would come due for payment", and Canada may reduce or terminate payments if authorities are amended or funding levels reduced, with 120 days' notice [7]. The four agreements are commitments of the executive that depend on annual appropriation, not statutory entitlements — the same structure, and the same vulnerability, as the Act itself.

### 3. What the agreements actually cover: contraception, diabetes drugs and devices, the specific products listed, and where coverage still stops

The benefit is two categories of drug plus a device stream, and the detail of the formularies matters more than the category labels suggest, because the provinces did not adopt identical lists and several products described as free are free only under conditions.

Start with what the federal government says the benefit is. Pharmacare "covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications" and "only" covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee [5]. Two exclusions follow immediately in the same passage: delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees are not covered [5]. That is a small but real qualification on the word "free." A resident who uses a delivery pharmacy, or who obtains a prescription through a pharmacist's prescribing authority rather than a physician's, faces a charge that pharmacare does not pay. For most people at a pharmacy counter the benefit is genuinely first-dollar; for some access routes it is not quite.

Eligibility is by residence and provincial insurance status rather than by age, income or insurance history. A person qualifies if they are a resident of a province or territory with an agreement in force and eligible for public health insurance there, with a valid prescription for a covered product [6]. Health Canada states the point that distinguishes this from every existing provincial drug program: "You're covered under pharmacare no matter your" age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [6]. People already covered by a federal or another provincial drug program keep that coverage rather than moving into pharmacare. Manitoba states it directly: "Clients with prescription medication coverage through a federal program are not eligible for coverage under MEPP." Those with 100 per cent coverage through the Non-Insured Health Benefits program or provincial employment and income assistance "are not eligible for MEPP and should continue to access their medications through these programs" [21]. BC's Plan NP is open to any resident enrolled in MSP, with exceptional coverage for those in the MSP wait period, but the same principle of not duplicating existing full coverage applies [22].

The drug lists in Annex A of each agreement are where the substance is, and they show a common core with provincial variation. The core across the four includes the fast-acting insulins (regular, lispro, aspart and glulisine), intermediate-acting isophane, the premixed human and lispro blends, long-acting glargine, metformin, glyburide and gliclazide, and SGLT2 and DPP-4 combinations such as empagliflozin-metformin and dapagliflozin [7][8]. Outside that core the lists diverge in ways the announcements do not mention: insulin detemir appears on some provincial lists but not BC's, and sitagliptin and sitagliptin-metformin appear only on Manitoba's [7][8].

For contraception the common core is the combined oral contraceptives by active ingredient (levonorgestrel, desogestrel, drospirenone, norethindrone and norgestimate with ethinylestradiol), progestin-only pills, medroxyprogesterone, etonogestrel implants, copper and progestogen IUDs, and the etonogestrel-ethinylestradiol vaginal ring [7][8]. The ring is the exception that shows how thin the commitment can be: Manitoba's Annex A entry for it reads "See note", and the note says only that Manitoba "will make best efforts to make this product (or an alternative) available over the course of the agreement" [8]. Best efforts is not coverage, and it is the kind of qualification that disappears from a press release.

The differences are instructive. Manitoba's list adds insulin degludec, glimepiride, acarbose, rosiglitazone, canagliflozin, repaglinide, glucagon and lixisenatide with insulin glargine [8]. BC's list does not carry all of those and instead specifies which brand-name versions are subject to its Low Cost Alternative policy [7]. The conditions of coverage vary as much as the products. Manitoba restricts a long list of its additions to Exception Drug Status, meaning the drug "is an eligible benefit only in Exception circumstances with prior approval from Manitoba" [8]. BC uses Special Authority for saxagliptin-metformin, linagliptin-metformin, pioglitazone, saxagliptin and linagliptin, and applies its Low Cost Alternative policy to brand-name metformin, gliclazide, dapagliflozin and several contraceptives, so that residents may be responsible for paying a portion of costs for the brand product where a cheaper generic is available free [7]. In practice BC removed most prior-approval requirements at launch — empagliflozin, empagliflozin-metformin, gliclazide, insulin glargine and topical estrogen no longer need Special Authority, and "No MHTs or contraceptives will require SA" [22]. The universal first-dollar standard therefore applies to at least one product in each category, not to every product a prescriber might choose.

Where a product is fully covered, BC's protection is strong: the Full Payment Policy means "pharmacies cannot charge a client for the medication or any service associated with the dispense" [22]. Manitoba's is weaker in one respect. It covers the cost of the product up to the lowest-cost interchangeable option plus "a professional fee of up to $14," but limits that fee to once a month for diabetes and HIV medications and once every three months for oral contraceptives, and states that any additional fees a pharmacy chooses to charge will not be covered [21]. For a Manitoban on daily dispensing, the medication is free and the pharmacy service may not be.

There are hard limits within the contraceptive benefit. Manitoba covers levonorgestrel emergency contraception to "Maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year" [8]. In Manitoba, copper IUDs are handled outside the pharmacy benefit altogether: the province lists them as available "at no cost directly from your health care provider", and states that "Copper IUDs dispensed through community pharmacies are not covered under MEPP" [21]. A Manitoban who fills a copper IUD prescription at a pharmacy pays for it and cannot be reimbursed [21]. BC covers copper and progestogen IUDs as regular benefits, with the brand-name vaginal ring subject to the Low Cost Alternative policy [7]. A woman in Manitoba and a woman in BC therefore face different out-of-pocket costs for the same contraceptive method, which is a real qualification on the claim that the first phase delivers universal access across the provinces that signed.

The device stream, Stream 2, is where the new coverage is most visible, though not uniformly new. BC's Stream 2 objectives are to "support hybrid closed-loop blood glucose monitor and insulin delivery systems; to include lancets for diabetic use; and to include additional supplies for insulin pump and glucose monitor users" [7], and BC's 2022-23 spending on all three categories was $0 [7]. What that money bought is now documented: from 1 April 2026 BC expanded coverage of alcohol wipes, lancets and blood and urine ketone strips, and it listed the mylife Ypsopump on 17 December 2025 and the Omnipod 5 hybrid closed-loop automated insulin delivery system on 1 April 2026, with the expansion attributed to federal pharmacare funding [22]. Manitoba's Stream 2 targets insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors, on which it already spent $1,449,593 in 2022-23 [8]. PEI's device baseline was $0, but its Stream 2 is aimed partly at lowering co-pay amounts rather than adding categories [9]. The amounts are modest — $37,839,549 for BC, $9,945,348 for Manitoba, $1,188,243 for PEI, $306,143 for Yukon — and in Manitoba's case they top up an existing program rather than create one.

What is not covered is as important as what is. The Act's payment authority runs to contraception and diabetes, but the provinces have used the agreements as a floor rather than a ceiling, and the result is that the benefit is wider than the federal categories in some places and narrower than the drug class in others. Manitoba is the clearest case: its Enhanced Pharmacare Program covers four categories — birth control, diabetes, HIV prevention and treatment, and hormone replacement therapy — and states that federal funding supports only the diabetes and birth control portions [21]. PrEP, PEP and antiretroviral therapy are free in Manitoba under a provincial decision the Pharmacare Act does not fund [21]. BC created a parallel Plan NP covering diabetes medications, menopausal hormone therapy and contraceptives, with the MHT benefit added by the province [22].

Within diabetes, the gap is the GLP-1 receptor agonists. Manitoba answers the question directly: "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories" [21]. Semaglutide is therefore not free under the program anywhere, while it is the drug driving the spending. CIHI measured spending on GLP-1 analogues and SGLT2 inhibitors at $868 million in 2022, representing 24% of total growth in public drug program spending, with Ozempic alone rising from $265 million in 2021 to $434 million in 2022 [17]. The SGLT2 inhibitors are on the provincial lists; the GLP-1 agonists largely are not, with the narrow exception of lixisenatide with insulin glargine on Manitoba's list as an Exception Drug Status benefit [8]. That exclusion is the single biggest constraint on the program's clinical reach, and it is a federal formulary decision rather than a provincial one.

On cost per patient, Health Canada's own framing gives the scale: insulin runs $900 to $1,700 a year and metformin about $100 [13]. A benefit built on those products improves equity at the pharmacy counter substantially — the person who was rationing insulin now is not — without much changing the trajectory of diabetes spending, because the expensive end of treatment sits outside the list.

The scale the program is meant to address is nonetheless large. About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes, and costs to the health care system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion in 2018, projected to surpass $39 billion by 2028 [13]. Those figures are for the whole disease, not for drugs, and no part of the pharmacare benefit is designed to bend them on its own.

### 4. How many people are actually using it: registrations, prescriptions filled, and what the government's own numbers do and do not show

No one has published a count of how many people have used national pharmacare. Not Health Canada, not the provinces, not the Canadian Institute for Health Information. The agreements do not require one before 2027. This is the single largest gap in the public record on this program, and it should be stated plainly rather than papered over with the government's reach estimates, which are projections and are routinely reported as if they were uptake.

What the government publishes is how many people a benefit could reach. At royal assent, Health Canada said the agreements would give "up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada free access to contraception" and that "the 3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes will have universal access to a suite of medications" [16]. For individual deals the same construction recurs: the Manitoba agreement "will support the reproductive freedom of nearly 350,000 Manitobans" and ensure "over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes can access essential medications" [12]; the BC deal was announced as covering more than 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 people with diabetes [11]. Every one of these is an estimate of the eligible population derived from provincial insurance rolls and diabetes prevalence, not a count of people who filled a prescription.

There is one place where the government has published an actual usage number, and it is not for pharmacare. Prince Edward Island's earlier federal-funded program, the $5 copay initiative launched in June 2023, generated a measurable result: PEI residents "saved over $2 million in out-of-pocket costs on more than 230,000 prescriptions" under the program, and the copay reduction applied to almost 60% of medications regularly used by Island residents [16]. That is what a reported uptake figure looks like — prescriptions and dollars, not eligible population — and it is notable that the pharmacare agreements, which are larger and more ambitious, do not require equivalent reporting.

The closest thing to real utilization data for a contraception benefit in Canada comes from British Columbia, but it describes the province's own program, which predates and is separate from the federal agreement. BC began providing free contraceptives to all residents on 1 April 2023. "In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception," and since the program began "more than 306,000 people have benefitted" [11]. That is the most useful number in the file, and it is instructive in two ways. It shows that a universal free-contraception benefit in a province of about 5.6 million people reaches roughly a quarter of a million people a year — a real, large effect. It also shows the gap between eligible population and users: BC's own announcement framed the federal deal as reaching 1.3 million people, while its actual provincial program served about 227,000 in a year. Eligibility and use are not the same thing, and the difference is roughly a factor of six.

The reason no pharmacare-specific count exists yet is written into the agreements. BC's obligation to report the savings delivered to residents on diabetes devices begins in fiscal year 2027-28, with the first report due 1 October 2027 [7]. The attested financial statements — which would show how much federal money was spent on products as distinct from administration, IT and evaluation — also begin in 2027-28 [7]. The agreements require provinces to publish which products are covered and how to access them, and to report their 2022-23 baseline spending, but not to report prescription volumes, beneficiary counts or out-of-pocket savings in the first two years of operation [7][8]. Manitoba's agreement requires it to publish the covered products by its implementation date and to report how Stream 2 money was used, but again no utilization data [8].

The timing makes this worse than it might sound. Two of the four implementation dates fell in 2025 — Manitoba on 15 April and PEI on 1 May — while the other two fall in 2026, BC on 1 March and Yukon between 15 April and 5 May [7][8][9][10]. Manitoba and PEI have therefore been operating for more than a year without publishing how many people they served, and BC and Yukon have barely started. Any claim that millions of Canadians are now using pharmacare is an inference from eligible population, not a measurement, and should be attributed as such.

What can be said with confidence is bounded by the size of the four jurisdictions. British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon together hold a minority of the Canadian population; Ontario, Quebec and Alberta alone hold most of it, and none of the three has signed. Even if every eligible resident of the four signatory jurisdictions used the benefit at the rate BC's own contraception program achieved, the program would be serving a few hundred thousand people a year, not the nine million the government's framing implies. That is my inference from BC's reported 227,000 set against the eligible-population figures the announcements give, not a figure any agency has published. The honest summary is that the program's reach is knowable in principle and unknown in fact, and will remain so until the 2027 reporting cycle or until a province chooses to publish.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer says a full national pharmacare program would cost, and exactly how it modelled that

The Parliamentary Budget Officer's estimate is the most methodologically transparent number in the Canadian pharmacare debate, and also the most frequently misquoted. Its most recent published costing models a single-payer universal drug plan built on Quebec's formulary and reports three different figures for the same program, each answering a different question. Getting them straight resolves most of the apparent disagreement with other estimates.

**The headline public-sector cost.** PBO estimates "the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28" [15]. That is the number to use when the question is what governments would have to find. It is explicitly a combined figure. PBO states: "As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs." [15] Any statement that the PBO put a federal price tag on pharmacare — $11.2 billion, $13.4 billion, or any other — misreads the report. The federal share depends on a cost-sharing formula that no government has settled.

**The gross cost to public drug plans.** PBO estimates "the gross cost incremental to that of public drug plans will be $14.8 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $17.3 billion in 2027-28" [15]. This is larger than the public-sector net figure because it is measured before the copayment revenues and the savings on existing direct federal spending are netted off. It is the number to use when the question is what the program spends on drugs, before asking who pays and what it displaces.

**The economy-wide result.** Total drug expenditure under Pharmacare would be $33.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28, but against the status quo PBO finds economy-wide savings of $1.4 billion rising to $2.2 billion, because Pharmacare spending grows at 5.3% a year against 5.8% under the baseline [15]. So the same report says the program costs the public sector $11.2 billion more and saves the country $1.4 billion. Both are true because the incidence differs: governments pay more, households and employers pay less, and the net is a modest saving. This is the mechanism the Hoskins council and the academic literature describe, quantified by the PBO.

The modelling choices behind those figures are what make them contestable, and they are stated in the report. The benefit design is universal and replaces existing public and private plans, using the RAMQ formulary as the national formulary, with "a $5 co-payment for all prescriptions of brand-name drugs" and exemptions for under-16s, students aged 16 to 18, people over 65, pregnant women, the physically disabled, and employment insurance and social assistance recipients [15]. The central behavioural assumption is stated in the report: "Prices borne directly by patients are expected to fall by 47 per cent to 100 per cent, which results in overall increases in the utilization of prescription drugs of 13.5 per cent." [15] That 13.5% is doing a lot of work. It is an estimate of induced demand — the prescriptions people fill once cost stops deterring them — and every dollar of the resulting cost increase depends on it. A skeptic could reasonably argue the elasticity is uncertain in either direction; the PBO's contribution is to state it and to make the result reproducible.

The most important feature of the report for current policy is that PBO costed three alternative formularies, and the results show the benefit package drives the number far more than any modelling parameter. Under a catastrophic formulary — one that covers only very high drug costs — "the incremental cost of a single-payer universal drug plan with a catastrophic formulary to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $1.8 billion and $2.0 billion in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [15]. Under an essential-medicines formulary, the result is startling in the other direction: PBO estimates drug expenditures "to be $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than the estimated spending under the baseline scenario in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [15]. Universal coverage of an essential medicines list would cost the public sector almost nothing net, because the drugs on such a list are mostly generics already priced low, so the added utilization is largely offset by the savings from displacing private spending and from stronger purchasing.

That last result is the direct quantitative bridge to the current program. The Pharmacare Act's first phase is closer to an essential-medicines design than to the comprehensive RAMQ design, and it is narrower still: two therapeutic categories rather than a full list. The PBO did not cost the contraception-and-diabetes benefit as such, but its formulary comparison establishes the shape of the answer — the first phase sits at the low end of the range, in the low single-digit billions at most for the whole country, not the $11.2 billion or $17.3 billion figures that get attached to "pharmacare" in general.

One methodological caution belongs here. PBO's baseline is a projection of what public drug plans would spend absent reform, and it depends on drug price growth, utilization trends and the entry of new products. The GLP-1 class illustrates the exposure: CIHI measured spending on GLP-1 analogues and SGLT2 inhibitors at $868 million in 2022, representing 24% of total growth in public drug program spending, with Ozempic alone rising from $265 million to $434 million in a year [17]. A formulary that excludes those drugs, as the provincial pharmacare lists do, is insulated from that growth; a comprehensive one is not. This is why the PBO's comprehensive estimate should be treated as a moving target rather than a fixed price, and why the essential-medicines estimate is more stable.

### 6. Other independent estimates — the Hoskins advisory council, C.D. Howe, CIHI's actual drug spending, academic pharmacoepidemiology — and why they diverge from the PBO

The cost estimates in circulation for national pharmacare are not competing answers to the same question. They differ because they ask different questions, count different things, and in some cases measure against different baselines. Reading them side by side as though they formed a single range, from roughly a billion dollars to tens of billions, produces a number that is wrong under every interpretation. What follows separates them by what they actually measure.

The most-cited official figure is the 2019 final report of the Advisory Council on the Implementation of National Pharmacare, chaired by Dr. Eric Hoskins. Its central estimate was incremental and staged:

> "We have estimated that it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines." [1]

The same report projected the cost of a comprehensive formulary rather than an essential-medicines one at $15.3 billion by 2027 [1]. Two features of that estimate matter for anyone comparing it to later figures. It is explicitly incremental — the additional cost on top of existing public and private spending, not gross program spending — and it is tied to a specific benefit design, an essential medicines list first, expanding later. An essential-medicines list covering roughly a hundred-odd products is a very different commitment from a comprehensive formulary, and the gap between $3.5 billion and $15.3 billion is mostly the gap between those two benefit designs rather than between two forecasts of the same thing. The council's work also assumed the savings from bulk purchasing and from displacing private insurance premiums would offset a substantial part of the gross cost; the incremental figure already nets those out.

The academic pharmacoepidemiology literature approaches the question from the opposite direction, asking not what a new program costs but what the country's total drug bill would do under universal public coverage. The most influential Canadian model, Morgan and colleagues in CMAJ in 2015, found that total spending would fall:

> "Universal public drug coverage would reduce total spending on prescription drugs in Canada by $7.3 billion (worst-case scenario $4.2 billion, best-case scenario $9.4 billion)." [3]

That is a 32% reduction in total Canadian prescription spending in the central case, and the paper's striking result is on the government side: a net government cost of roughly $958 million, because universal public coverage replaces existing public spending, private insurance premiums and out-of-pocket payments rather than adding a new layer on top [3]. This is the estimate most often quoted by pharmacare advocates, and it is arithmetically defensible on its own terms — but it answers a different question than a federal budget officer does. It is a system-wide net figure for Canada as a whole, covering all payers, not a federal expenditure line. A federal government cannot book the elimination of private insurance premiums as savings to its own bottom line, even where those savings are real to households and employers. Comparing the Morgan net government cost to a PBO gross federal cost is a category error, and it is made routinely in Canadian commentary on this file.

The practical consequence is that the published estimates are best understood as a set of figures indexed to benefit design and to whose budget is being counted, not as a disagreement about facts. Three distinctions do most of the work. Gross program cost versus incremental cost: gross counts every dollar the program spends, incremental counts only what is added after existing spending is displaced. Federal cost versus system cost: the federal treasury bears only the federal share, while system cost nets out savings to households, employers and provincial governments. Essential medicines versus comprehensive formulary: the benefit package determines the number more than any modelling assumption does, which is why the Hoskins council could publish two figures a decade apart for the same program.

A fourth distinction is measurement versus projection, and it is the one this report can speak to least well. The figures above are all forward-looking models. Actual Canadian prescription drug spending is measured annually by the Canadian Institute for Health Information, and that series is the correct denominator against which any projection should be sanity-checked: a projected national program cost that implies implausible per-capita drug spending is a modelling error, not a finding. This report has not yet established the current CIHI total or the latest PBO modelling, so the comparison cannot be completed here.

What can be said with confidence is that the divergence between the published estimates is mostly explicable rather than contradictory, and that the largest single driver is benefit design. A government that funds contraception and diabetes drugs, as the Pharmacare Act currently authorises, is operating at the very bottom of this range — the first phase of the Hoskins council's own staged design, and far below either the $15.3 billion comprehensive figure or the gross costs implied by a full national program. The cost question that matters for the current program is therefore not the headline national pharmacare number at all, but the much smaller figure attached to the bilateral agreements themselves.

label: evidence, studies
q: What does the evidence say about school smartphone bans: which jurisdictions (Ontario, England, the Netherlands, Australian states and others) have adopted them, what have evaluations measured about learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong is that evidence?

report.title: School smartphone bans: which jurisdictions have adopted them, what evaluations measured on learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong that evidence is

review.sentence: Crucially, England does not legislate.
review.why: The DfE page now states "This guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026" and describes itself as "statutory guidance", with schools to follow it from 1 September 2026 — so England's rule is no longer non-statutory. The later sentence "guidance plus inspection pressure, not statute" repeats the same outdated claim.

review.sentence: Germany is also the clearest case of a country that did not converge: most German schools restrict phones under their own rules without a national prohibition [8].
review.why: The UNESCO source says only that several Länder have banned phones in primary and special-needs schools and that Brandenburg, Bremen, Hesse and Schleswig-Holstein have tightened regulations and are "increasingly relying on bans". It says nothing about most German schools restricting phones under their own rules, and does not present Germany as a case of non-convergence.

review.sentence: Bans were rolled out state by state from 2020 rather than nationally [1].
review.why: The cited note says the opposite about scope: "In Australia, since 2020, phone bans have been progressively rolled out nationally." Nothing in the note attributes the rollout to individual states or says it was not national, so the section inverts its own source.

review.sentence: The study was powered to detect a difference of 3 points, the accepted minimum clinically important difference, so a clinically meaningful effect was ruled out, not merely missed.
review.why: SMART Schools is a cross-sectional comparison of schools that had chosen their policies, and its authors state that causality cannot be drawn, that reverse causality cannot be ruled out and that selection bias and unmeasured confounding are risks; a null association here cannot "rule out" a policy effect. The power calculation also assumed an SD of 6.8, whereas the observed WEMWBS SD was 9, so the achieved precision was lower than planned.

review.sentence: The restriction acts on in-school minutes; the association runs through total daily and nightly use.
review.why: This mechanism is the writer's, not the source's. SMART Schools reports that in-school smartphone/social media time was itself significantly associated with higher anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, disruptiveness and worse attainment; the paper does not locate the harm exclusively in out-of-school hours.

review.sentence: South Australia, measuring bullying with PISA's seven-item self-report index of verbal, physical, relational and extortion bullying, found no policy effect.
review.why: The source's bullying items ask about the past 12 months ("Bullying (During past 12 months)"), while follow-up came one month after baseline, so the follow-up score largely re-measures pre-ban experience. The study could not register policy-driven change in bullying, so it should not be presented as a test that found no bullying effect.

review.sentence: The equity story that animates much of the policy case — that bans protect the most vulnerable — is not supported by the one study that tested it directly.
review.why: SMART Schools also tested whether the policy–outcome association differed by deprivation (school IDACI), sex, year group and ethnicity and found no significant interactions, so South Australia is not "the one study" to test the equity hypothesis; the section's own cited UK study did too.

review.sentence: But it is the only US study that attempts a causal design on mental health, and its direction matches the English cross-section and the Australian natural experiment.
review.why: Saffer's abstract claims only to be "the first to examine the causal effects of school smartphone bans on the mental health of youth in the US", and stresses the results are "preliminary evidence only"; "the only US study" is a wider scope claim the source does not make.

review.sentence: The baseline imbalance deserves emphasis — the no-ban group had significantly lower bullying and higher academic engagement before the ban [1] — which the authors say did not alter the pattern of results, but which limits how much weight a two-school-group comparison can carry.
review.why: The section never mentions that implementation was partial: self-reported compliance with the South Australian ban was 87% at baseline and 79.9% at follow-up, and being older, a heavier social media user, or using a phone at school before the ban predicted non-compliance. Weak implementation is the main alternative explanation for a null and it is left out.

review.sentence: No study in this set measures cyberbullying separately from bullying with a design capable of attributing change to the policy; the Spanish result uses official reports, the Australian one a combined online/offline index.
review.why: The South Australian survey did record online bullying separately (its bullying item asks whether bullying occurred online, offline or both, and the results table reports online-only and combined categories), so the design captured cyberbullying separately even though the analysis used a combined index; the claim should be about the analysis, not about what was measured.

sentences.sentence: UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report team, which has monitored school phone rules since 2023, reported in March 2026 that **114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide**, up from "less than 1 in 4 countries (24%)" in June 2023 and 40% by early 2025 [8].

That figure is a count of national instruments, not of enforced practice, and the same monitoring exercise is careful to say the picture "is more nuanced than a simple shift toward prohibition" [8]. **England.** The Department for Education's guidance states the default plainly: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [5].

Schools are told to prohibit phones and "other smart technology with similar functionality" — the guidance gives the ability to receive notifications or to record audio and video as the test — "throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [5].

Exceptions are written in: disabled pupils under the Equality Act 2010, where access is a reasonable adjustment and denial "may be a breach of the school's duty"; pupils with medical conditions such as glucose monitors; young carers; and sixth-form students [5].

The guidance as first published was advisory; the DfE's own page now carries a banner reading "This guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026", with schools to begin following it from 1 September 2026 [5].

What is statutory is the duty to have a prohibiting policy, not a prescribed enforcement method: "There are a number of ways in which schools can ensure that they are mobile phone-free, and it is for headteachers to decide how best to achieve this within their own unique contexts" [5] — lockers, handing phones to staff at the start of the day, confiscation and detention are all offered as acceptable routes, and a search power exists where schools list phones as a prohibited item [5].

UNESCO's description of the English model as "strengthened guidance encouraging schools to prohibit mobile phones during the school day", with the expectation "reinforced through school inspection frameworks, yet the policy leaves implementation decisions to individual schools" [8], was accurate for the period before June 2026.

The SMART Schools study, whose fieldwork ran from November 2022 to November 2023, likewise described UK policy at that time as "non-statutory guidance recommending prohibiting phones in schools, where prohibiting phone use is left to the school's discretion" [6].

The point that survives all these changes is the one that matters for evaluation: English "bans" are policies schools design and enforce themselves, and schools that choose strict regimes differ from schools that do not. **Ontario.** Ontario's rule is age-tiered rather than a flat prohibition: students in Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobile devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher, while students in Grade 6 and below may not use them at school during the school day without a teacher's permission [7].

The instrument is a provincial policy for schools, and the tiering means the youngest children face the strictest rule and adolescents the loosest. **Australia.** Bans have spread nationally since 2020, though the instrument sits with state and territory governments: as the South Australian study's introduction puts it, "In Australia, since 2020, phone bans have been progressively rolled out nationally" [1].

South Australia's version, announced in November 2022 and in force from Term 1 2023 in public secondary schools, is among the strictest documented forms: "the policy requires students in all government schools to keep their personal devices, including mobile phones, off and away between the start and end of each school day" [1].

That is a whole-day, in-school custody rule, not merely a classroom rule — which is why the South Australian evaluation is the most informative Australian test of a genuinely restrictive policy. **France.** France introduced "one of the most widely cited early bans on mobile phones in schools, prohibiting their use in primary and lower secondary education" [8].
As of March 2026, "39 states now have statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring school districts to adopt policies restricting phone use in classrooms (24)" [8].

"In Germany, several Länder, including Bavaria, Saarland, and Thuringia, have banned smartphones in primary and special needs schools" [8], while Brandenburg, Bremen, Hesse and Schleswig-Holstein have tightened their regulations and are, in UNESCO's phrasing, "increasingly relying on bans" [8] — a patchwork rather than a national rule.

Argentina's ban applies in the province of Buenos Aires rather than nationally, and subnational restrictions also appear in Armenia, Indonesia, Thailand and North Macedonia [8]. **Regulation without prohibition.** A substantial group of governments has legislated process rather than prohibition.

UNESCO lists Comoros, Colombia, Estonia, Lithuania, Iceland, Peru, Indonesia, Serbia, Poland and the Philippines as countries that "recently adopted national regulations requiring schools to develop policies restricting phone use, without imposing a strict nationwide prohibition" [8].

New national bans continue to appear — Bolivia, Costa Rica, Croatia, Georgia, Maldives and Malta are the most recent additions [8] — while France is now examining whether its 2018 settlement needs tightening [8].

Almost every policy citation in this literature traces back to one study, and that study has been contradicted by the largest attempt to replicate it. **The claim that started it.** The study by Beland and Murphy — published as *Ill Communication: Technology, distraction & student performance* in *Labour Economics* in 2016, after earlier working-paper versions — examined "data from 90 schools in the United Kingdom that had implemented a phone ban between the years 2006 and 2010" [1].
The effects were twice as large for low-achieving students, and we found no impact on high achieving students" [2].
In contrast to Beland and Murphy's study, Kessel et al. reported no improvement in student performance in schools with a phone ban" [1].
However, two of these studies found this improvement only applied to disadvantaged or low-achieving students" [3].
This means we can be reasonably confident in these results" [3].

Its authors found that "adolescents attending schools with restrictive phone policies did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour, compared to pupils who attended schools where phone use was permitted during the school day" [6].

That is a weaker claim, but it is the claim most policy advocates actually make, and it is not supported. **Academic engagement and self-reported learning.** The South Australian natural experiment measured academic engagement rather than test scores, using a three-item scale from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (motivation to study, ability to concentrate, achievement in studies) after dropping a stress item that broke internal consistency [1].

There was a statistically significant ban-by-time interaction, with engagement rising in the ban group (d = 0.28) but not in the no-ban group (d = 0.09) — yet the follow-up comparison showed no significant difference between groups on academic engagement (d = 0.03, 95% CI −0.14 to 0.20) [1].
The authors themselves concluded the ban and no-ban schools "either did not differ significantly, or there were minimal differences" on academic engagement [1].

Comparing 20 restrictive schools with 10 permissive schools, pupils in restrictive schools had lower phone time "during school time" by an adjusted mean difference of −0.67 hours (95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and lower social media time by −0.54 hours (95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) — "but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [6].

The authors make the inference explicit: "One potential explanation for this lack of observed difference, is that restrictive school phone policies did not lower the overall time adolescents spent on their phones/social media" [6]. **Does it reduce classroom disruption?** SMART Schools measured teacher-reported classroom behaviour and attainment and found that pupils in restrictive schools "did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour, compared to pupils who attended schools where phone use was permitted during the school day" [6].

First, the baseline prevalence was tiny: "Problematic phone use was reported by 2.6% of the sample" [1] — with so few cases, the outcome had almost no room to fall, and a null here is weak evidence of no effect.

Second, the decline that occurred was not attributable to the ban: "there was a significant main effect of time for problematic phone use indicating that, collapsed across condition, problematic phone use decreased over time" [1], while there was no significant main effect of condition and no condition-by-time interaction [1].

Third, the authors' interpretation is mechanistic rather than statistical: "Imposing access restrictions may not affect the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive problematic phone use" [1]. **Compliance is the binding constraint.** A ban that is not complied with cannot produce effects, and the South Australian compliance data are unusually candid.
At baseline 87% of pupils in ban schools reported following the ban [1]; by follow-up the adherence figure was 79.9% [1].
Non-compliance was not random: "Being older, a more frequent user of social media, using phone at school before the ban, and experiencing bullying, were associated with phone ban non-compliance" [1].

This is a selection problem inside the treatment, and it biases every intention-to-treat estimate in this literature toward zero. **The American null on exposure.** The first US causal study of state school smartphone bans, an NBER working paper by Henry Saffer using synthetic difference-in-differences on the National Survey of Children's Health from 2016 to 2024, examined screentime as an outcome and reported that "these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing" [4].
The nearest measures are teacher-rated disruptive behaviour [6], a three-item self-report engagement scale [1], and self-reported phone minutes [6].

Bullying and mental health are the outcomes most often cited by governments introducing bans, and they are the outcomes on which the best-controlled studies find the least. **The problem the policy is aimed at is real and large.** The SMART Schools authors set out the trend their study was designed to test: "In the UK, rates of probable mental disorders (mostly anxiety and depression) for those aged 8–16 rose from 12.5% in 2017 to 20.3% in 2023" [6].
Mean WEMWBS was 47 (SD = 9), "with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [6].
The study was powered to detect a 3-point difference, the accepted minimum clinically important difference, assuming an SD of 6.8 [6].

The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [6].

The null was not confined to wellbeing. the authors report no differences in adolescents' self-reported mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, or their motives for using social media between restrictive and permissive schools [6].

Sleep, physical activity, attainment and teacher-reported disruptive behaviour were also indistinguishable [6]. **The tension inside that study.** SMART Schools also found that phone and social media time is associated with harm: "We observed that increased time spent on phones/social media is significantly associated with worsened outcomes for mental health and wellbeing, physical activity and sleep, and attainment and disruptive behaviour" [6].
SMART Schools does not itself locate the harm outside school hours; it reports that in-school phone and social media time was also associated with higher anxiety, depression and problematic use [6].

The authors' own reading is that "This study does not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, given that no differences were observed in mental, physical, and academic outcomes for adolescents attending schools that permit, versus restrict phone use" [6], while the associations they found justify addressing phone use "as part a more holistic approach" [6].

The first clause is a finding; the second is a policy inference, and should be labelled as one. **The American causal test agrees.** Saffer's synthetic difference-in-differences analysis of the National Survey of Children's Health found "no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing" [4].
Saffer describes it as the first study to examine the causal effects of school smartphone bans on youth mental health in the US, and stresses that the results are preliminary evidence only [4].

Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella examined bans in two Spanish regions in 2015 using PISA data from 2006 to 2018 and officially reported bullying cases from the Spanish Ministry of Education between 2012 and 2017; as summarised in the South Australian study's introduction, "Among students aged 12–17 years, there was a 15–18% reduction in bullying incidence following the ban, and a 10–18% reduction among 15- to 17-year-olds" [1].
"There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups" [1], and there was no significant condition-by-time interaction [1].

The authors' summary: "There was a small decline in bullying and problematic phone use over time in both school groups regardless of phone ban, suggesting the phone ban may not necessarily underlie these changes" [1].

First, the ban was only partly followed: 87% of pupils in ban schools reported compliance at baseline, falling to 79.9% at follow-up, and non-compliance was predicted by being older, being a heavier social media user, having used a phone at school before the ban, and having experienced bullying [1].

Second, the groups were not balanced to begin with — the no-ban group had significantly lower bullying and higher academic engagement before the ban [1] — which the authors say did not alter the pattern of results, but which limits how much weight a five-school, two-group comparison can carry. **No subgroup was helped more.** The South Australian team tested whether the ban worked better for disadvantaged, distressed or dissatisfied students, the hypothesis most often advanced by advocates.

"Notably, these analyses showed that there were no significant main effects of condition or condition × time interactions on psychological distress and life satisfaction" [1], and no three-way interaction with socioeconomic status, psychological distress or life satisfaction for any outcome [1].

SMART Schools introduced interactions between policy and pupil sex, ethnicity, year group and school deprivation (IDACI) into its models [6], and found no significant moderation. **What has not been measured.** The South Australian survey did record whether bullying happened online, offline or both, but the published analysis uses a combined index, so online-only bullying was measured and then not analysed separately [1].
The Spanish result rests on official reports rather than pupil reports [1].
Beland and Murphy is the archetype: 90 UK schools that adopted bans between 2006 and 2010, with the timing of adoption supplying the comparison [1].

This is the most likely explanation for why the result failed to replicate: the Swedish study covered 1,086 schools and found nothing [1], and there is no way to know from either paper whether the "bans" were comparable policies. *Phase-in natural experiments* are the best available design and the rarest.
The study was preregistered, used a 2×2 repeated-measures design, and recruited 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up across five public secondary schools [1].

Its weaknesses are equally specific: five schools, a one-month follow-up, only 597 students completing both waves [1], and a baseline imbalance in which the no-ban group had lower bullying and higher academic engagement before any policy applied [1].

The authors' own verdict is "limited to no short-term benefits" [1] — short-term is doing real work in that sentence. *Cross-sectional comparisons* are what SMART Schools is, and its authors say plainly what that costs: "A limitation is that the study design is cross sectional which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about causality and reverse causality cannot be ruled out.
Furthermore, there is a risk of selection bias and unmeasured confounding in this study" [6].
Its compensating strength is scale and measurement: 30 schools, 1,227 pupils, a validated primary outcome, accelerometer-measured sleep and activity, and propensity stratification in recruitment [6].

When it finds an adjusted mean difference of −0.48 on WEMBBS with a confidence interval from −2.05 to 1.06 [6], it rules out a clinically meaningful association in a way no small study can. *Synthetic difference-in-differences on national survey data* is the newest entrant and, so far, the least powered.

Saffer's NBER paper is candid that "Currently, there are data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only" [4].

A preliminary null from an underpowered design should not be counted as evidence of no effect; it should be counted as an unfinished study. **Where the studies agree.** Three findings recur across designs, countries and outcome measures, and agreement of this kind is worth more than any single result: 1. **Bans change when and where phones are used, not how much.** English restrictive schools showed 0.67 fewer hours of in-school phone use but no difference across the week [6]; the US analysis found no reduction in screentime [4]; South Australia found problematic use declining equally in both groups [1].

Three different data sources, one consistent pattern. 2. **The largest, best-powered tests of attainment find nothing on average.** The Swedish nationwide cohort and a Norwegian study covering 30% of schools both found no academic difference, which the review authors say means "we can be reasonably confident in these results" [3].
