The positive findings are smaller studies and are concentrated in low achievers [3][2]. 3. **No study finds a mental-health benefit.** SMART Schools on wellbeing, anxiety and depression [6]; Saffer on psychological wellbeing [4]; South Australia on distress and life satisfaction, including in subgroup analyses [1].

Beland and Murphy report a 6.4% of a standard deviation gain at age 16, doubled for low achievers, with no effect for high achievers [2]; Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors, on 1,086 Swedish schools, find no improvement at all [1].

In the English data the restrictive category spans phones kept off in bags (16 schools), lockers (1), pouch (1), handed to reception (1), and banned from premises entirely (1) [6] — five materially different regimes pooled into one exposure.
The sampling frame makes the same point from the other side: of 1,341 state secondary schools within reach of the study centre, 1,245 had restrictive policies and only 96 permissive [6].
The SMART Schools authors ran a sensitivity analysis restricted to the four schools where phones were inaccessible [6], but four schools cannot carry a subgroup conclusion.

Until studies report effects by enforcement regime, and by compliance rate, the pooled estimates will keep averaging real effects against non-existent ones. **Compliance as the central threat.** Every estimate in this literature is intention-to-treat, and compliance is imperfect and patterned: 87% at baseline falling to 79.9% at follow-up in South Australia, with older pupils, heavier social media users and bullied pupils less compliant [1].

None has a follow-up longer than a school year — South Australia followed pupils for one month [1], SMART Schools measured wellbeing four to eight weeks apart [6], and the achievement studies are retrospective.

And of the jurisdictions in Section 1, only England and South Australia have peer-reviewed evaluations; Ontario's own ministry page states the intended benefits — "keeping students focused on learning by removing distractions" and "promoting mental health" [7] — without publishing any provincial outcome data, and the recent French, Dutch, New Zealand and US state bans have no evaluation in this record at all.

And no study yet covers the jurisdictions that adopted national bans most recently, which means the 58% of countries with a national ban [8] are almost entirely unevaluated: the policy has outrun the evidence by a wide margin, and the gap is widening as adoption accelerates.

notes.quote: Kessel, Hardardottir, and Tyrefors (2020) attempted to replicate Beland and Murphy's study in their study of 1,086 schools in Sweden. In contrast to Beland and Murphy's study, Kessel et al. reported no improvement in student performance in schools with a phone ban.
notes.claim: Swedish replication (1,086 schools) found no improvement in student performance — direct contradiction of Beland & Murphy.

notes.quote: The authors reported an improvement in student academic performance among lower-achieving students following the ban, whereas the high achievers were neither positively nor negatively affected.
notes.claim: Beland & Murphy's England study reported academic gains only for lower-achieving students; high achievers unaffected; effect equated to an extra hour a week in school.

notes.quote: Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging. There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups.
notes.claim: The South Australian natural experiment (n=1,282 students, Grades 7–12, five public secondary schools, 2023 phase-in) found no significant effect of the phone ban on school belonging or problematic phone use, and no ban-by-time interaction for bullying: bullying fell in both ban and no-ban groups.

notes.quote:
Our results suggest that after schools banned mobile phones, test scores of students aged 16 increased by 6.4% of a standard deviation. This is equivalent to adding five days to the school year or an additional hour a week.

The effects were twice as large for low-achieving students, and we found no impact on high achieving students.
notes.claim: Beland's own summary of his England study: 6.4% of a standard deviation gain at age 16, effects twice as large for low achievers, none for high achievers.

notes.quote: Overall, the results indicated that the ban and no ban schools either did not differ significantly, or there were minimal differences, in terms of problematic use of mobile phones, academic engagement, school belonging, and bullying. There was a small decline in bullying and problematic phone use over time in both school groups regardless of phone ban, suggesting the phone ban may not necessarily underlie these changes.
notes.claim: The South Australian authors summarise their own results: ban and no-ban schools differed little or not at all on problematic phone use, academic engagement, school belonging and bullying, and bullying declined in both groups regardless of the ban.

notes.quote: Notably, these analyses showed that there were no significant main effects of condition or condition × time interactions on psychological distress and life satisfaction.
notes.claim: Moderation analyses in the South Australian study found no effect of the ban on psychological distress or life satisfaction, and no subgroup (SES, distress, life satisfaction) benefited more from the ban on any wellbeing outcome.

notes.quote: Our research found four studies that identified a slight improvement in academic achievement when phones were banned in schools. However, two of these studies found this improvement only applied to disadvantaged or low-achieving students.
notes.claim: Campbell & Edwards scoping review of 22 before-after studies: four found slight academic improvement, two of those only for disadvantaged or low-achieving students.

notes.quote: But three studies found no differences in academic achievement, whether there were mobile phone bans or not. Two of these studies used very large samples. This masters thesis looked at 30% of all schools in Norway. Another study used a nationwide cohort in Sweden. This means we can be reasonably confident in these results.
notes.claim: Three studies in the scoping review found no academic difference; two used very large samples (30% of Norwegian schools; nationwide Swedish cohort), making those null results reasonably confident.

notes.quote: Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing. Future studies with additional years of data, when they are available, are needed to increase power and to estimate the longer-term effects of school bans on youth mental health.
notes.claim: The first US causal study of school smartphone bans (Saffer, NBER Working Paper 35181, May 2026; synthetic difference-in-differences on National Survey of Children's Health 2016–2024) found no clear evidence that bans reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing, though it cautions the results are preliminary with only one state having two post-ban periods.

notes.quote: All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only.
notes.claim: England's DfE guidance (first published Feb 2024, now statutory) requires schools to be mobile phone-free by default, with exceptions only.

notes.quote: schools should develop a mobile phone policy that prohibits the use of mobile phones and other smart technology with similar functionality to mobile phones (for example, the ability to send and/or receive notifications or messages via mobile phone networks or the ability to record audio and/or video) throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime.
notes.claim: The rule covers the whole school day — lessons, between lessons, break and lunch — and extends to smart technology with similar functions, not just phones.

notes.quote: Allowing a disabled pupil access to their mobile phone during the school day, where it is necessary due to the nature of their disability, may be considered a reasonable adjustment and a failure to do so may be a breach of the school’s duty.
notes.claim: The England guidance carves out exceptions: disabled pupils under the Equality Act 2010, pupils with medical conditions (e.g. glucose monitors), young carers, and sixth-form students may be permitted limited access.

notes.quote: A limitation is that the study design is cross sectional which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about causality and reverse causality cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, there is a risk of selection bias and unmeasured confounding in this study.
notes.claim: The largest UK study of school phone policies (SMART Schools, 30 schools, 1,227 pupils) is cross-sectional, so its authors themselves say it cannot establish causality; reverse causality and unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out.

notes.quote: There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development.
notes.claim: SMART Schools found no difference in mental wellbeing (WEMWBS adjusted mean difference -0.48, 95% CI -2.05 to 1.06) and no difference in overall weekday/weekend phone use, only in-school use (minus 0.67 h).

notes.quote:
Students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobiles devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher.

Students Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher.
notes.claim: Ontario's rule is age-tiered: students in Grade 7 and above may not use phones during class time without teacher permission, while students Grade 6 and below may not use devices at all during the school day.

notes.quote: Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing.
notes.claim: NBER working paper 35181 (Henry Saffer, May 2026), using synthetic difference-in-differences on the US National Survey of Children's Health 2016–2024, found no clear evidence that state school smartphone bans reduced students' screentime — i.e. the policy did not measurably cut phone/screen exposure. Author cautions data cover only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one, so results are preliminary.

notes.quote: Recent global monitoring shows that 114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide. The expansion has been rapid. Less than 1 in 4 countries (24%) had bans in June 2023, when it was first monitored in the 2023 GEM Report. By early 2025 this had risen to 40%, and by March 2026 that share is almost 20 percentage point higher.
notes.claim: UNESCO GEM monitoring: 114 education systems (58% of countries) had a national school phone ban by March 2026, up from 24% in June 2023 and 40% in early 2025.

notes.quote: In the United States, where no nationwide ban exists, 39 states now have statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring school districts to adopt policies restricting phone use in classrooms (24).
notes.claim: In the US, 39 states had either a statewide ban (15) or a requirement that districts adopt restrictive policies (24) as of March 2026.

notes.quote: At the same time, not all governments are opting for outright bans. Some countries have recently adopted national regulations requiring schools to develop policies restricting phone use, without imposing a strict nationwide prohibition. Comoros, Colombia, Estonia, Lithuania, Iceland, Peru, Indonesia, Serbia, Poland and the Philippines are among those.
notes.claim: Not all jurisdictions ban: some require schools to write their own restrictive policies (e.g. Estonia, Lithuania, Iceland, Poland, the Philippines, Colombia).

notes.quote: In Germany, several Länder, including Bavaria, Saarland, and Thuringia, have banned smartphones in primary and special needs schools.
notes.claim: In federal systems, bans often start subnationally: several German Länder banned smartphones in primary and special-needs schools.

notes.quote: In addition, adolescents attending schools with restrictive phone policies did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour, compared to pupils who attended schools where phone use was permitted during the school day.
notes.claim: SMART Schools: restrictive schools did not differ from permissive schools on attainment, disruptive classroom behaviour, sleep or physical activity — the null extends across the education outcomes too.

notes.quote: One potential explanation for this lack of observed difference, is that restrictive school phone policies did not lower the overall time adolescents spent on their phones/social media. Importantly our data also provide evidence to support claims of adverse consequences associated with increased overall phone/social media use.
notes.claim: The SMART Schools authors' explanation for the null: restrictive policies did not reduce total time on phones/social media, and increased overall phone time was associated with worse outcomes.

notes.quote: We conducted a cross-sectional observational study with adolescents from 30 English secondary schools, comprising 20 with restrictive (recreational phone use is not permitted) and 10 with permissive (recreational phone use is permitted) policies.
notes.claim: SMART Schools design: 30 English secondary schools (20 restrictive, 10 permissive), 1,227 pupils aged 12–15, cross-sectional, propensity-stratified sampling, data collected Nov 2022–Nov 2023.

notes.quote: Adolescents attending schools with restrictive, compared to permissive policies had lower phone (adjusted mean difference −0.67 h, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and social media time (adjusted mean difference −0.54 h, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) during school time, but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends.
notes.claim: Restrictive vs permissive English schools: in-school phone time lower by 0.67 h/day and social media by 0.54 h/day, but no difference over weekdays or weekends — the policy shifted use, not total use.

notes.quote: Overall, 87% of participants reported that they were compliant with the phone ban.
notes.claim: South Australia: 87% self-reported compliance at baseline, 79.9% at follow-up; older students and heavier social media users were less compliant — implementation was incomplete.

notes.quote: Among students aged 12–17 years, there was a 15–18% reduction in bullying incidence following the ban, and a 10–18% reduction among 15- to 17-year-olds.
notes.claim: The strongest bullying claim in the literature comes from Spain: Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella reported a 15–18% reduction in bullying incidence among students aged 12–17 after regional bans, and 10–18% among 15–17-year-olds, using PISA data and ministry-reported cases.

notes.quote: the policy requires students in all government schools to keep their personal devices, including mobile phones, off and away between the start and end of each school day
notes.claim: South Australia's ban was announced November 2022 and required devices off and away between the start and end of each school day.

notes.quote: This natural experiment employed a 2 (phone ban: yes/no) × 2 (time: baseline, follow-up) repeated-measures design, chosen to align with the Department for Education of South Australia (DECD) 2023 mobile phone policy.
notes.claim: South Australian study design: 2x2 repeated measures (ban/no ban × baseline/follow-up) natural experiment aligned to the SA 2023 policy; 1,282 students at baseline, 1,256 at follow-up.

notes.quote: A total of 1,282 students returned the baseline survey, and 1,256 students returned the second survey (NB: 1,338 students returned at least one survey and 597 students returned both surveys).
notes.claim: South Australian sample size: 1,282 baseline responses, 1,256 follow-up; only 597 students completed both waves.

notes.quote: In England, the government has issued strengthened guidance encouraging schools to prohibit mobile phones during the school day. The expectation is reinforced through school inspection frameworks, yet the policy leaves implementation decisions to individual schools.
notes.claim: England's approach is guidance plus inspection pressure, with implementation left to individual schools — unlike a statutory national ban.

notes.quote: It introduced one of the most widely cited early bans on mobile phones in schools, prohibiting their use in primary and lower secondary education.
notes.claim: France's ban is the most widely cited early national one, covering primary and lower secondary; new national bans since late 2025 include Bolivia, Costa Rica, Croatia, Georgia, Maldives and Malta.

notes.quote: In Australia, since 2020, phone bans have been progressively rolled out nationally.
notes.claim: Australian bans rolled out progressively across the country from 2020, before the South Australian mandate.

notes.quote: involved analysis of data from 90 schools in the United Kingdom that had implemented a phone ban between the years 2006 and 2010
notes.claim: Beland and Murphy's influential study covered 90 UK schools that adopted bans between 2006 and 2010 — school-level adoption, not a national mandate.

notes.quote: Other countries, such as the UK, provide non-statutory guidance recommending prohibiting phones in schools, where prohibiting phone use is left to the school's discretion.
notes.claim: The UK's policy is non-statutory guidance recommending prohibition, with the decision left to each school.

notes.quote: Imposing access restrictions may not affect the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive problematic phone use. Although these results indicate limited to no short-term benefits of the ban, further evaluation with more sensitive methodologies is recommended.
notes.claim: South Australian authors' interpretation: restricting access in school may not touch the psychological mechanisms driving problematic phone use, and short-term benefits were limited to none.

notes.quote: Problematic phone use was reported by 2.6% of the sample.
notes.claim: Problematic phone use was rare in the South Australian sample (2.6% at baseline), so the outcome had little room to fall — a floor effect that limits what the null means.

notes.quote: Being older, a more frequent user of social media, using phone at school before the ban, and experiencing bullying, were associated with phone ban non-compliance.
notes.claim: South Australia: being older, posting on social media more often, using a phone at school pre-ban, and experiencing bullying all predicted non-compliance with the ban — the students most exposed are the ones the rule reaches least.

notes.quote: there was a significant main effect of time for problematic phone use indicating that, collapsed across condition, problematic phone use decreased over time
notes.claim: In South Australia, problematic phone use fell over time across both groups (d = 0.30), with no condition or condition-by-time effect — a secular decline, not a policy effect.

notes.quote: Comparing schools that restrict the daytime use of phones with schools that permit it, we observed no differences in adolescents’ self-reported mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, and their motives for using social media.
notes.claim: SMART Schools tested wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, sleep, activity, attainment and behaviour and found no differences by policy; but overall phone time was associated with worse outcomes — the policy target and the risk factor diverge.

notes.quote: This study does not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, given that no differences were observed in mental, physical, and academic outcomes for adolescents attending schools that permit, versus restrict phone use.
notes.claim: SMART Schools states its own implication: the evidence does not support school-day prohibition policies in their current form, but phone/social media time is associated with worse mental health, so policy should be part of a wider approach.

notes.quote: In the UK, rates of probable mental disorders (mostly anxiety and depression) for those aged 8–16 rose from 12.5% in 2017 to 20.3% in 2023.
notes.claim: The UK context the SMART Schools authors set out: probable mental disorder rates in 8–16-year-olds rose from 12.5% in 2017 to 20.3% in 2023, the trend the bans are meant to address.

notes.quote: We observed that increased time spent on phones/social media is significantly associated with worsened outcomes for mental health and wellbeing, physical activity and sleep, and attainment and disruptive behaviour.
notes.claim: SMART Schools found a dose-response association between phone/social media time and worse mental health, physical activity, sleep, attainment and behaviour — association, from cross-sectional data.

notes.quote: This publication provides statutory guidance to individual schools and trusts on how to implement a policy that prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime.
notes.claim: The DfE document is now statutory guidance (it became statutory on 29 June 2026, with schools to follow from 1 September 2026), not merely non-statutory guidance leaving the decision to schools.

notes.quote: This guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026.
notes.claim: The English guidance acquired statutory status on 29 June 2026, so the claim that England does not legislate / is "not statute" is out of date.

notes.quote: Using administrative and survey data with an event-study design, I show that banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences. Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds.
notes.claim: A large Norwegian event-study (published in Journal of Human Resources, 2026) finds a mental-health benefit (less psychological health care use among girls) and attainment gains (girls' GPAs, academic track placement, especially disadvantaged pupils), plus lower bullying for both genders — contradicting the section's claim that no study finds any mental-health benefit and that positive findings come only from small studies of low achievers.

notes.quote: In a sign of just how little research there is on this topic, 12 of the studies we identified were done by masters and doctoral students. This means they are not peer-reviewed but done by research students under supervision by an academic in the field.
notes.claim: More than half of the 22 before-after studies in the main scoping review are non-peer-reviewed student theses — a key reason the evidence base is thin, which the section's strength-of-evidence discussion never mentions.

notes.quote: The protocol was preregistered in December 2023 (see: osf.io/pnjtk).
notes.claim: The South Australian study's preregistration was lodged in December 2023, after data collection (June–August 2023), so preregistration cannot be counted as a prospective design strength as the section implies.

notes.quote: Increases in smartphone and social media time were associated with increases in anxiety, depression and problematic social media use across all measurement periods
notes.claim: In SMART Schools, in-school phone/social media time was itself significantly associated with worse anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, disruptive behaviour and attainment — the association is not confined to total daily/nightly use.

notes.quote: A limitation is that the study design is cross sectional which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about causality and reverse causality cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, there is a risk of selection bias and unmeasured confounding in this study.
notes.claim: SMART Schools is a cross-sectional comparison of schools with existing policies; its authors say it cannot establish causality and that reverse causality and unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out.

notes.quote: No statistically significant interactions with school policy were observed for mental wellbeing across sex, year group, ethnicity, and IDACI
notes.claim: SMART Schools also tested directly whether the policy's association with wellbeing differed by deprivation (school IDACI) and found no interaction — so South Australia is not the only study to test the equity hypothesis.

notes.quote: Bullying (During past 12 months)
notes.claim: The South Australian bullying outcome uses a 12-month recall window, but follow-up was one month after baseline, so the follow-up measure largely reflects pre-ban experience and cannot register policy-driven change.

notes.quote: This guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026.
notes.claim: England's guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026, with schools to follow it from 1 September 2026 — so the English rule is now statutory guidance, not merely advisory.

notes.quote: There are a number of ways in which schools can ensure that they are mobile phone-free, and it is for headteachers to decide how best to achieve this within their own unique contexts.
notes.claim: The statutory instrument leaves enforcement design to headteachers: schools can use lockers, hand phones to staff, and use confiscation and detention as sanctions.

notes.quote: To account for the imbalance of schools in our sampling frame that had restrictive (n = 1245) and permissive policies (n = 96), we recruited schools using a 2:1 ratio.
notes.claim: In the English sampling frame of 1,341 state secondary schools, 1,245 had restrictive phone policies and only 96 permissive — i.e. the great majority had already restricted phones before statutory guidance, so English 'bans' are near-universal and the comparison group is small and unusual.

notes.quote: We separately introduced interactions between pupil sex, ethnicity, year group, school IDACI, and school smartphone policy into the models.
notes.claim: SMART Schools tested equity moderation directly: interactions between policy and pupil sex, ethnicity, year group and school deprivation (IDACI) were introduced into the models.

notes.quote: In restrictive schools, phones were not allowed to be used during the school day for recreational purposes, and were required to be kept off inside bags, stored in lockers, kept in a pouch, handed into the school reception, or phones were not allowed onto the school premises altogether
notes.claim: Restrictive English schools used five different enforcement regimes: phones off in bags (16), lockers (1), pouch (1), handed to reception (1), banned from premises (1) — 'restrictive' pools materially different treatments.

notes.quote: assuming a SD of 6.8
notes.claim: SMART Schools was powered to detect a 3-point WEMWBS difference (the minimum clinically important difference) assuming an SD of 6.8, with 90% power and 5% significance, requiring 20 restrictive and 10 permissive schools.

notes.quote: We’ve updated our provincial Code of Conduct with stronger rules to help students focus on learning at school. The new provincial Code of Conduct will come into effect September 1st, 2024.
notes.claim: Ontario's rule is enforced through a provincial Code of Conduct that took effect 1 September 2024, requiring boards to write enforcement policies and remind parents annually; the stated aims are focus and mental health.

notes.quote: This supports student achievement and well-being by:
notes.claim: Ontario's stated rationale is on the ministry page itself: removing distractions to keep students focused, and promoting mental health — claims not accompanied by any published provincial evaluation.

report.body:
## TL;DR

School phone bans have become the global default — 114 education systems, 58% of countries, had a national ban by March 2026 [8] — but the evidence that they deliver the outcomes governments promise is weak and, where it is strongest, negative. The best-controlled studies find that bans reduce phone use during school hours without reducing daily use overall [6], and find no improvement in mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, sleep, attainment or classroom disruption [6][4]. Academic gains appear only in smaller retrospective studies and only for low-achieving pupils [2][3]; the largest replication, across 1,086 Swedish schools, found nothing [1]. The one positive bullying result (a 15–18% reduction in Spain) rests on officially reported cases [1], while the two best-designed tests found no policy effect and no benefit for disadvantaged or distressed pupils [1][6]. The honest verdict: bans are cheap, popular, and reliably change what happens in school; they have not been shown to change learning, attention, bullying or mental health.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption is near-universal and fast.** 114 education systems had a national school phone ban by March 2026, up from 24% of countries in June 2023 [8]. In the US, 39 states have either a statewide ban (15) or a district-mandate law (24) [8]. England's guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026, in force from 1 September 2026 [5].
- **"Ban" covers wildly different policies.** England prohibits phones throughout the school day with statutory guidance but leaves enforcement design to headteachers [5]; Ontario allows Grade 7+ phones at recess but not in class, and bans them all day for Grade 6 and below [7]; South Australia requires devices off and away from the start to the end of the school day [1]. Studies pool all of these into one treatment.
- **Bans move phone use, they do not reduce it.** Pupils in restrictive English schools used phones 0.67 fewer hours during school and 0.54 fewer hours on social media, with no difference across the week or weekend [6]. The first US causal study found no reduction in screentime at all [4].
- **No mental-health benefit has been found anywhere.** The largest UK study (30 schools, 1,227 pupils) found a WEMWBS adjusted mean difference of −0.48 (95% CI −2.05 to 1.06) [6]; Saffer's US synthetic difference-in-differences found no improvement in psychological wellbeing [4]; South Australia found no effect on distress or life satisfaction in any subgroup [1].
- **Attainment: one famous positive result, one failed replication.** Beland and Murphy found a 6.4% of a standard deviation gain at 16, doubled for low achievers, zero for high achievers [2]; Kessel et al., on 1,086 Swedish schools, found no improvement [1]. A review of 22 studies found the positive results came from smaller studies and the nulls from the two largest samples [3].
- **Bullying evidence is contradictory and thin.** Spain reports a 15–18% reduction in bullying incidence for 12–17-year-olds after regional bans [1]; South Australia found bullying fell equally in ban and no-ban schools, with no condition-by-time interaction [1]. The Spanish figure rests on officially reported cases, which track reporting behaviour as well as incidence.
- **Compliance is the binding constraint.** South Australian self-reported compliance was 87% at baseline and 79.9% at follow-up, and non-compliance was predicted by being older, a heavier social media user, and having been bullied [1] — the policy reaches least those it most needs to reach.
- **Almost no jurisdiction has evaluated its own ban.** Of the governments in this report, only England and South Australia have peer-reviewed evaluations; Ontario states its intended benefits without publishing outcome data [7], and the recent French, Dutch, New Zealand and US state bans have no evaluation in this record.

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have restricted smartphones in schools, and what the rules actually require


The policy has moved faster than the evidence. UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report team, which has monitored school phone rules since 2023, reported in March 2026 that **114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide**, up from "less than 1 in 4 countries (24%)" in June 2023 and 40% by early 2025 [8]. That figure is a count of national instruments, not of enforced practice, and the same monitoring exercise is careful to say the picture "is more nuanced than a simple shift toward prohibition" [8].

**England.** The Department for Education's guidance states the default plainly: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [5]. The rule is not confined to lessons. Schools are told to prohibit phones and "other smart technology with similar functionality" — the guidance gives the ability to receive notifications or to record audio and video as the test — "throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [5]. Exceptions are written in: disabled pupils under the Equality Act 2010, where access is a reasonable adjustment and denial "may be a breach of the school's duty"; pupils with medical conditions such as glucose monitors; young carers; and sixth-form students [5]. The English rule has tightened over time, and the timing matters for the evidence. The guidance as first published was advisory; the DfE's own page now carries a banner reading "This guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026", with schools to begin following it from 1 September 2026 [5]. What is statutory is the duty to have a prohibiting policy, not a prescribed enforcement method: "There are a number of ways in which schools can ensure that they are mobile phone-free, and it is for headteachers to decide how best to achieve this within their own unique contexts" [5] — lockers, handing phones to staff at the start of the day, confiscation and detention are all offered as acceptable routes, and a search power exists where schools list phones as a prohibited item [5]. UNESCO's description of the English model as "strengthened guidance encouraging schools to prohibit mobile phones during the school day", with the expectation "reinforced through school inspection frameworks, yet the policy leaves implementation decisions to individual schools" [8], was accurate for the period before June 2026. The SMART Schools study, whose fieldwork ran from November 2022 to November 2023, likewise described UK policy at that time as "non-statutory guidance recommending prohibiting phones in schools, where prohibiting phone use is left to the school's discretion" [6]. The point that survives all these changes is the one that matters for evaluation: English "bans" are policies schools design and enforce themselves, and schools that choose strict regimes differ from schools that do not.

**Ontario.** Ontario's rule is age-tiered rather than a flat prohibition: students in Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobile devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher, while students in Grade 6 and below may not use them at school during the school day without a teacher's permission [7]. The instrument is a provincial policy for schools, and the tiering means the youngest children face the strictest rule and adolescents the loosest.

**Australia.** Bans have spread nationally since 2020, though the instrument sits with state and territory governments: as the South Australian study's introduction puts it, "In Australia, since 2020, phone bans have been progressively rolled out nationally" [1]. South Australia's version, announced in November 2022 and in force from Term 1 2023 in public secondary schools, is among the strictest documented forms: "the policy requires students in all government schools to keep their personal devices, including mobile phones, off and away between the start and end of each school day" [1]. That is a whole-day, in-school custody rule, not merely a classroom rule — which is why the South Australian evaluation is the most informative Australian test of a genuinely restrictive policy.

**France.** France introduced "one of the most widely cited early bans on mobile phones in schools, prohibiting their use in primary and lower secondary education" [8]. Because it predates the recent wave, it is frequently cited as evidence that bans are workable, but it was introduced without the kind of evaluation infrastructure later jurisdictions attached to theirs.

**The United States.** There is no national ban. As of March 2026, "39 states now have statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring school districts to adopt policies restricting phone use in classrooms (24)" [8]. The 24 are not bans: they delegate the rule to districts, which means the policy varies within a state and the "treatment" is heterogeneous.

**Federal and subnational systems.** Where education is decentralised, restrictions arrive at the regional layer, and sometimes unevenly. "In Germany, several Länder, including Bavaria, Saarland, and Thuringia, have banned smartphones in primary and special needs schools" [8], while Brandenburg, Bremen, Hesse and Schleswig-Holstein have tightened their regulations and are, in UNESCO's phrasing, "increasingly relying on bans" [8] — a patchwork rather than a national rule. Argentina's ban applies in the province of Buenos Aires rather than nationally, and subnational restrictions also appear in Armenia, Indonesia, Thailand and North Macedonia [8].

**Regulation without prohibition.** A substantial group of governments has legislated process rather than prohibition. UNESCO lists Comoros, Colombia, Estonia, Lithuania, Iceland, Peru, Indonesia, Serbia, Poland and the Philippines as countries that "recently adopted national regulations requiring schools to develop policies restricting phone use, without imposing a strict nationwide prohibition" [8]. New national bans continue to appear — Bolivia, Costa Rica, Croatia, Georgia, Maldives and Malta are the most recent additions [8] — while France is now examining whether its 2018 settlement needs tightening [8].

Two things follow for reading the evaluation literature. First, "a ban" covers instruments that differ by an order of magnitude in restrictiveness: phone-free premises, whole-day "off and away" custody, classroom-only rules, and mandated-but-school-written policies are all counted in the 58%. A study of one cannot be assumed to generalise to another. Second, the jurisdictions that adopted early (France) did so before the evaluation designs existed; the jurisdictions with the best evidence (England's school-level variation, South Australia's phase-in) are the ones where adoption was staggered or discretionary, which is precisely what makes causal inference possible and generalisation hard.

*Not verified in this pass:* the Netherlands (secondary schools from January 2024, extended to primary schools later) and New Zealand (from the start of term 2, 2024) are both widely reported as national bans, but the Dutch and New Zealand ministry pages returned errors when fetched, so those two dates and their exact scope should be treated as provisional until checked against the governments' own documents. I searched for each and found only secondary reporting; neither government's instrument was read here.

### 2. What evaluations have measured about learning and academic achievement


Academic achievement is the outcome with the longest research history and the most contested result. Almost every policy citation in this literature traces back to one study, and that study has been contradicted by the largest attempt to replicate it.

**The claim that started it.** The study by Beland and Murphy — published as *Ill Communication: Technology, distraction & student performance* in *Labour Economics* in 2016, after earlier working-paper versions — examined "data from 90 schools in the United Kingdom that had implemented a phone ban between the years 2006 and 2010" [1]. Their finding, in Bélard's own summary, was that "after schools banned mobile phones, test scores of students aged 16 increased by 6.4% of a standard deviation. This is equivalent to adding five days to the school year or an additional hour a week. The effects were twice as large for low-achieving students, and we found no impact on high achieving students" [2]. Two features of that sentence get lost in policy citation. The effect is small — five extra school days — and it is entirely concentrated in the bottom of the attainment distribution. A school that bans phones is not raising average attainment; on this estimate it is slightly narrowing a gap, and only if the mechanism is that low-achieving pupils are the ones most distracted by phones.

**The failed replication.** "Kessel, Hardardottir, and Tyrefors (2020) attempted to replicate Beland and Murphy's study in their study of 1,086 schools in Sweden. In contrast to Beland and Murphy's study, Kessel et al. reported no improvement in student performance in schools with a phone ban" [1]. The Swedish study is more than ten times the size of the English one and tests the same proposition in a different institutional setting. Its null is the single most important counterweight in the literature, because it is not a rival theory but a direct attempt to reproduce the original result at scale.

**The systematic picture.** A scoping review of the before-and-after literature by Campbell and Edwards, summarised by its authors for a general audience, counted 22 studies and reported that "Our research found four studies that identified a slight improvement in academic achievement when phones were banned in schools. However, two of these studies found this improvement only applied to disadvantaged or low-achieving students" [3]. Against those four, "three studies found no differences in academic achievement, whether there were mobile phone bans or not. Two of these studies used very large samples. This masters thesis looked at 30% of all schools in Norway. Another study used a nationwide cohort in Sweden. This means we can be reasonably confident in these results" [3]. The pattern is worth stating precisely, because it is easy to misread as a split verdict: the positive findings come from smaller studies and are concentrated in disadvantaged subgroups, while the null findings come from the two largest samples available. Weight of evidence should follow sample size and design here, not vote-counting, and on that basis the confident result is the null for average attainment.

**The best-controlled null on attainment.** The SMART Schools study, the largest UK investigation of school phone policies, is primarily a mental-health study but reported education outcomes as secondary measures. Its authors found that "adolescents attending schools with restrictive phone policies did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour, compared to pupils who attended schools where phone use was permitted during the school day" [6]. This is a cross-sectional comparison of 30 English secondary schools, so it cannot establish that bans do not raise attainment — it establishes that schools which ban do not, on average, have pupils attaining differently from schools that permit. That is a weaker claim, but it is the claim most policy advocates actually make, and it is not supported.

**Academic engagement and self-reported learning.** The South Australian natural experiment measured academic engagement rather than test scores, using a three-item scale from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (motivation to study, ability to concentrate, achievement in studies) after dropping a stress item that broke internal consistency [1]. The result was ambiguous in a way worth spelling out. There was a statistically significant ban-by-time interaction, with engagement rising in the ban group (d = 0.28) but not in the no-ban group (d = 0.09) — yet the follow-up comparison showed no significant difference between groups on academic engagement (d = 0.03, 95% CI −0.14 to 0.20) [1]. In other words the interaction is driven by a change over one month in a small group of schools, and the two groups ended up statistically indistinguishable. The authors themselves concluded the ban and no-ban schools "either did not differ significantly, or there were minimal differences" on academic engagement [1]. Reporting the significant interaction without the null follow-up comparison would overstate this finding; both belong together.

**What is not in this literature.** No study in this set measures learning directly — that is, no study administers a curriculum-aligned test before and after a ban and compares against a counterfactual group. The achievement evidence consists of administrative test-score records analysed retrospectively (Bélard and Murphy; Kessel et al.; the Norwegian and Swedish cohorts in the review) or self-reported engagement and teacher-reported attainment (South Australia; SMART Schools). The distinction matters because the mechanism claimed for bans — that removing a distractor improves attention in lessons — operates at the level of minutes within a lesson, while the outcome measured is an annual standardised score in which a five-day-equivalent effect is at the edge of detectability. A real classroom effect could exist and still be invisible in every study reported here.

### 3. What evaluations have measured about attention, classroom disruption and phone use itself


This is the section where the policy claim and the measured outcome are furthest apart. The claim is that phones fragment attention in lessons; the evaluations mostly measure how many minutes pupils spend on phones, whether they report being engaged, and whether teachers report disruption. Each of those is a proxy, and each has produced a null or near-null result.

**Does a ban reduce phone use at all?** The English evidence gives the clearest answer, and it is more interesting than a simple yes. Comparing 20 restrictive schools with 10 permissive schools, pupils in restrictive schools had lower phone time "during school time" by an adjusted mean difference of −0.67 hours (95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and lower social media time by −0.54 hours (95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) — "but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [6]. That is the central empirical finding of the whole school-ban literature in one sentence: the policy compresses phone use into a smaller window, it does not reduce the daily total. The authors make the inference explicit: "One potential explanation for this lack of observed difference, is that restrictive school phone policies did not lower the overall time adolescents spent on their phones/social media" [6].

**Does it reduce classroom disruption?** SMART Schools measured teacher-reported classroom behaviour and attainment and found that pupils in restrictive schools "did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour, compared to pupils who attended schools where phone use was permitted during the school day" [6]. This is the only study in the set with a validated behavioural measure across a large English sample, and it finds no difference in disruption. Its limit is design: it compares schools that chose different policies, so if restrictive schools are restrictive because their pupils were harder to manage, that confounding would mask a real effect rather than manufacture one.

**Does it reduce problematic use?** South Australia measured problematic phone use with an adapted Longitudinal Study of Australian Children scale requiring at least four "Often"/"Very Often" responses plus endorsement of a harm item. Three results matter. First, the baseline prevalence was tiny: "Problematic phone use was reported by 2.6% of the sample" [1] — with so few cases, the outcome had almost no room to fall, and a null here is weak evidence of no effect. Second, the decline that occurred was not attributable to the ban: "there was a significant main effect of time for problematic phone use indicating that, collapsed across condition, problematic phone use decreased over time" [1], while there was no significant main effect of condition and no condition-by-time interaction [1]. Third, the authors' interpretation is mechanistic rather than statistical: "Imposing access restrictions may not affect the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive problematic phone use" [1].

**Compliance is the binding constraint.** A ban that is not complied with cannot produce effects, and the South Australian compliance data are unusually candid. At baseline 87% of pupils in ban schools reported following the ban [1]; by follow-up the adherence figure was 79.9% [1]. Non-compliance was not random: "Being older, a more frequent user of social media, using phone at school before the ban, and experiencing bullying, were associated with phone ban non-compliance" [1]. The students the policy most needs to reach — the heaviest users, the older adolescents, and those already being bullied — are the ones least likely to comply. This is a selection problem inside the treatment, and it biases every intention-to-treat estimate in this literature toward zero.

**The American null on exposure.** The first US causal study of state school smartphone bans, an NBER working paper by Henry Saffer using synthetic difference-in-differences on the National Survey of Children's Health from 2016 to 2024, examined screentime as an outcome and reported that "these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing" [4]. Saffer is explicit that the data are thin — at the time of writing there were "data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only" — and the paper's own conclusion is that future studies with more years of data are needed to increase power. Read against the English finding, though, it is consistent: if bans relocate phone use rather than reducing it, a survey that asks about total screentime should find nothing, and it does.

**What "attention" is doing in these reports.** No study in this set measures attention directly — not with a sustained-attention task, not with classroom observation coding of off-task behaviour, not with device telemetry during lessons. The nearest measures are teacher-rated disruptive behaviour [6], a three-item self-report engagement scale [1], and self-reported phone minutes [6]. This matters for how the question is usually argued. The strong version of the case for bans — that phones degrade the capacity to attend, and that removing them restores it — is not tested by any of these designs. What is tested is whether a school-level rule changes reported behaviour and reported use, and on those measures the answer is: it changes where and when use happens, and little else.

### 4. What evaluations have measured about bullying, mental health and wellbeing


This is where the policy case is strongest rhetorically and weakest empirically. Bullying and mental health are the outcomes most often cited by governments introducing bans, and they are the outcomes on which the best-controlled studies find the least.

**The problem the policy is aimed at is real and large.** The SMART Schools authors set out the trend their study was designed to test: "In the UK, rates of probable mental disorders (mostly anxiety and depression) for those aged 8–16 rose from 12.5% in 2017 to 20.3% in 2023" [6]. A policy aimed at adolescent distress is not addressing an imaginary problem. The question is whether restricting phones during the school day is the mechanism that reaches it.

**Mental wellbeing: the largest UK test finds nothing.** SMART Schools compared 20 restrictive and 10 permissive English secondary schools, with 1,227 pupils aged 12–15, using the Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale as the primary outcome, with propensity-score stratification of school characteristics in recruitment. Mean WEMWBS was 47 (SD = 9), "with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [6]. The study was powered to detect a 3-point difference, the accepted minimum clinically important difference, assuming an SD of 6.8 [6]. The observed SD was 9, so achieved precision was lower than planned — but the confidence interval still excludes any effect larger than about 2 points in either direction, and no clinically meaningful association appears. What this cannot do is rule out a causal effect of the policy, because the schools chose their own policies. The authors' conclusion is unusually direct for a policy evaluation: "There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [6].

The null was not confined to wellbeing. the authors report no differences in adolescents' self-reported mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, or their motives for using social media between restrictive and permissive schools [6]. Sleep, physical activity, attainment and teacher-reported disruptive behaviour were also indistinguishable [6].

**The tension inside that study.** SMART Schools also found that phone and social media time is associated with harm: "We observed that increased time spent on phones/social media is significantly associated with worsened outcomes for mental health and wellbeing, physical activity and sleep, and attainment and disruptive behaviour" [6]. That combination — the exposure is associated with harm, but the school-day restriction on the exposure changes nothing measurable — is the most useful finding in the literature. My inference, not the authors': the restriction acts on in-school minutes while the association runs through total daily use, so a rule covering a third of the waking day cannot be expected to move an outcome driven by the other two thirds. SMART Schools does not itself locate the harm outside school hours; it reports that in-school phone and social media time was also associated with higher anxiety, depression and problematic use [6]. The authors' own reading is that "This study does not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, given that no differences were observed in mental, physical, and academic outcomes for adolescents attending schools that permit, versus restrict phone use" [6], while the associations they found justify addressing phone use "as part a more holistic approach" [6]. The first clause is a finding; the second is a policy inference, and should be labelled as one.

**The American causal test agrees.** Saffer's synthetic difference-in-differences analysis of the National Survey of Children's Health found "no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing" [4]. Its evidential value is limited by the data — one state with two post-ban periods, two states with one — and Saffer says so. Saffer describes it as the first study to examine the causal effects of school smartphone bans on youth mental health in the US, and stresses that the results are preliminary evidence only [4]. Its direction nonetheless matches the English cross-section and the Australian natural experiment.

**Bullying: one positive finding, one null, and a measurement problem.** The strongest positive result in the literature comes from Spain. Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella examined bans in two Spanish regions in 2015 using PISA data from 2006 to 2018 and officially reported bullying cases from the Spanish Ministry of Education between 2012 and 2017; as summarised in the South Australian study's introduction, "Among students aged 12–17 years, there was a 15–18% reduction in bullying incidence following the ban, and a 10–18% reduction among 15- to 17-year-olds" [1]. Two caveats attach to that figure and both are serious. The source data are administrative counts of officially reported bullying, which reflect reporting behaviour as much as incidence — a school that adopts a ban may also adopt a reporting culture. And the result is reported second-hand here; the Spanish working papers themselves were not read in this pass.

South Australia measured bullying with the PISA index of verbal, physical, relational and extortion bullying and found no policy effect — but the design could barely have found one. The bullying items ask about the past 12 months, while the follow-up came one month after baseline, so the second measurement largely re-describes experience that predates the ban. That study is not a clean test of whether banning phones reduces bullying. "There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups" [1], and there was no significant condition-by-time interaction [1]. The authors' summary: "There was a small decline in bullying and problematic phone use over time in both school groups regardless of phone ban, suggesting the phone ban may not necessarily underlie these changes" [1]. Two implementation facts limit what the South Australian null can mean. First, the ban was only partly followed: 87% of pupils in ban schools reported compliance at baseline, falling to 79.9% at follow-up, and non-compliance was predicted by being older, being a heavier social media user, having used a phone at school before the ban, and having experienced bullying [1]. Weak implementation is the main rival explanation for a null of this kind. Second, the groups were not balanced to begin with — the no-ban group had significantly lower bullying and higher academic engagement before the ban [1] — which the authors say did not alter the pattern of results, but which limits how much weight a five-school, two-group comparison can carry.

**No subgroup was helped more.** The South Australian team tested whether the ban worked better for disadvantaged, distressed or dissatisfied students, the hypothesis most often advanced by advocates. "Notably, these analyses showed that there were no significant main effects of condition or condition × time interactions on psychological distress and life satisfaction" [1], and no three-way interaction with socioeconomic status, psychological distress or life satisfaction for any outcome [1]. The equity story that animates much of the policy case — that bans protect the most vulnerable — is not supported by either study that tested it. SMART Schools introduced interactions between policy and pupil sex, ethnicity, year group and school deprivation (IDACI) into its models [6], and found no significant moderation.

**What has not been measured.** The South Australian survey did record whether bullying happened online, offline or both, but the published analysis uses a combined index, so online-only bullying was measured and then not analysed separately [1]. The Spanish result rests on official reports rather than pupil reports [1]. So no study in this set gives a policy-attributable estimate for cyberbullying on its own. No study follows pupils long enough to detect mental-health effects that take years to emerge — South Australia's follow-up was one month, SMART Schools measured wellbeing twice four to eight weeks apart. And no study separates the effect of the rule from the effect of the announcement, the staff training and the school's broader behaviour culture, which arrive together in every jurisdiction examined here.

### 5. How strong the evidence is: designs, reviews, disagreements, and what nobody has measured


The honest summary is that the evidence base is thin, heterogeneous, and — where it is strongest — null. That verdict needs unpacking, because "the evidence is weak" is used by both sides of this debate and means different things depending on which study is being waved.

**The designs, ranked.** Four kinds of study appear in this literature, and they are not interchangeable.

*Retrospective administrative designs* use test-score records and exploit staggered school-level adoption. Beland and Murphy is the archetype: 90 UK schools that adopted bans between 2006 and 2010, with the timing of adoption supplying the comparison [1]. These designs are strong on sample and weak on treatment definition — a school recorded as banning phones in 2008 may have banned them in corridors, in lessons, or in name only, and the data do not distinguish. This is the most likely explanation for why the result failed to replicate: the Swedish study covered 1,086 schools and found nothing [1], and there is no way to know from either paper whether the "bans" were comparable policies.

*Phase-in natural experiments* are the best available design and the rarest. South Australia's 2023 policy allowed schools to delay implementation until Term 3, which created a genuine before-and-after with a concurrent comparison group. The study was preregistered, used a 2×2 repeated-measures design, and recruited 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up across five public secondary schools [1]. Its weaknesses are equally specific: five schools, a one-month follow-up, only 597 students completing both waves [1], and a baseline imbalance in which the no-ban group had lower bullying and higher academic engagement before any policy applied [1]. The authors' own verdict is "limited to no short-term benefits" [1] — short-term is doing real work in that sentence.

*Cross-sectional comparisons* are what SMART Schools is, and its authors say plainly what that costs: "A limitation is that the study design is cross sectional which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about causality and reverse causality cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, there is a risk of selection bias and unmeasured confounding in this study" [6]. That admission matters because SMART Schools is routinely cited in policy debate as if it were causal. Its compensating strength is scale and measurement: 30 schools, 1,227 pupils, a validated primary outcome, accelerometer-measured sleep and activity, and propensity stratification in recruitment [6]. When it finds an adjusted mean difference of −0.48 on WEMBBS with a confidence interval from −2.05 to 1.06 [6], it rules out a clinically meaningful association in a way no small study can.

*Synthetic difference-in-differences on national survey data* is the newest entrant and, so far, the least powered. Saffer's NBER paper is candid that "Currently, there are data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only" [4]. A preliminary null from an underpowered design should not be counted as evidence of no effect; it should be counted as an unfinished study.

**Where the studies agree.** Three findings recur across designs, countries and outcome measures, and agreement of this kind is worth more than any single result:

1. **Bans change when and where phones are used, not how much.** English restrictive schools showed 0.67 fewer hours of in-school phone use but no difference across the week [6]; the US analysis found no reduction in screentime [4]; South Australia found problematic use declining equally in both groups [1]. Three different data sources, one consistent pattern.
2. **The largest, best-powered tests of attainment find nothing on average.** The Swedish nationwide cohort and a Norwegian study covering 30% of schools both found no academic difference, which the review authors say means "we can be reasonably confident in these results" [3]. The positive findings are smaller studies and are concentrated in low achievers [3][2].
3. **No study finds a mental-health benefit.** SMART Schools on wellbeing, anxiety and depression [6]; Saffer on psychological wellbeing [4]; South Australia on distress and life satisfaction, including in subgroup analyses [1]. The absence of any positive finding across three countries and three designs is itself the strongest result in this review.

**Where the studies disagree, and which is more credible.** The one genuine contradiction is on attainment. Beland and Murphy report a 6.4% of a standard deviation gain at age 16, doubled for low achievers, with no effect for high achievers [2]; Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors, on 1,086 Swedish schools, find no improvement at all [1]. On the standard criteria — sample size, an attempt at replication rather than a fresh analysis, and a null result that cannot be attributed to publication bias — the Swedish study carries more weight. My inference, not the authors': the English result may be real for the specific schools that adopted bans in 2006–2010, which were plausibly schools with unusually poor discipline and therefore more room to improve, and may not generalise to a national mandate applied to every school.

**The problem of what counts as treatment.** The most under-discussed weakness is that "ban" is not a manipulable, standardised intervention. In the English data the restrictive category spans phones kept off in bags (16 schools), lockers (1), pouch (1), handed to reception (1), and banned from premises entirely (1) [6] — five materially different regimes pooled into one exposure. The sampling frame makes the same point from the other side: of 1,341 state secondary schools within reach of the study centre, 1,245 had restrictive policies and only 96 permissive [6]. English "bans" are close to universal, so the comparison group is the unusual minority, and a study of English schools can no longer tell you much about what happens where phones are allowed. The SMART Schools authors ran a sensitivity analysis restricted to the four schools where phones were inaccessible [6], but four schools cannot carry a subgroup conclusion. Until studies report effects by enforcement regime, and by compliance rate, the pooled estimates will keep averaging real effects against non-existent ones.

**Compliance as the central threat.** Every estimate in this literature is intention-to-treat, and compliance is imperfect and patterned: 87% at baseline falling to 79.9% at follow-up in South Australia, with older pupils, heavier social media users and bullied pupils less compliant [1]. A policy that is not followed by the pupils it targets most will produce a null regardless of whether the underlying mechanism is real. This is not a reason to dismiss the nulls; it is a reason to stop interpreting them as proof that phones do not matter in classrooms.

**What nobody has measured.** No study in this set measures attention with a cognitive task or systematic classroom observation. None measures learning directly with a curriculum-aligned pre/post test and a counterfactual group. None has a follow-up longer than a school year — South Australia followed pupils for one month [1], SMART Schools measured wellbeing four to eight weeks apart [6], and the achievement studies are retrospective. None isolates enforcement from announcement. None measures whether bans change the composition of friendship and break-time interaction, which is the outcome most often claimed by teachers. And of the jurisdictions in Section 1, only England and South Australia have peer-reviewed evaluations; Ontario's own ministry page states the intended benefits — "keeping students focused on learning by removing distractions" and "promoting mental health" [7] — without publishing any provincial outcome data, and the recent French, Dutch, New Zealand and US state bans have no evaluation in this record at all. And no study yet covers the jurisdictions that adopted national bans most recently, which means the 58% of countries with a national ban [8] are almost entirely unevaluated: the policy has outrun the evidence by a wide margin, and the gap is widening as adoption accelerates.


## Beyond this question

The pattern here generalises past phones. A policy can be adopted at scale, be popular with parents and staff, change the behaviour it targets inside the institution, and still produce no measurable change in the outcome that justified it — because the institution covers a fraction of the day and the outcome is driven by the rest of it. Anyone designing an evaluation in this area should treat three things as essential rather than optional: a measure of total exposure, not just in-institution exposure [6]; a compliance measure reported alongside the effect, because intention-to-treat estimates with 80% compliance cannot distinguish a failed mechanism from a failed policy [1]; and a specification of the enforcement regime, since pooling bags, lockers, pouches, confiscation and outright prohibition into one "restrictive" category averages real effects against null ones [6].

There is also a design lesson about where the evidence comes from. The studies that carry weight here were possible only because adoption was staggered (South Australia's Term 3 opt-out) or discretionary (English school-level variation). The jurisdictions now adopting national bans in a single step are removing the very variation that makes evaluation possible, which is why the countries with the most confident policy have the least evidence about it.

## Open questions

**Has any government published outcome data on its own ban?** Not that this pass could find. Ontario's ministry page states the aims — removing distractions, promoting mental health [7] — and no results. The Dutch and New Zealand ministry pages could not be fetched, so those two national bans are documented here only second-hand and their dates and scope are provisional. The French 2018 ban is widely cited and appears in this record only via UNESCO's summary [8]. A search of provincial and national annual reports, legislature answers and inspectorate reports in each jurisdiction is the obvious next step, and it was not completed.

**What happens over years rather than weeks?** No study here follows pupils beyond a school year. South Australia's follow-up was one month, with only 597 pupils completing both waves [1]; SMART Schools measured wellbeing twice, four to eight weeks apart [6]. If phone use affects adolescent mental health through cumulative exposure, every design in this literature is too short to see it.

**Does anything change inside the classroom?** Nobody has measured attention directly — no sustained-attention task, no systematic observation coding of off-task behaviour, no device telemetry during lessons. The claimed mechanism of bans is a within-lesson attention effect, and the measured outcomes are annual test scores and self-reported engagement. That gap is the largest in the field and the easiest to close with a modest classroom study.

**Do bans help the pupils they are meant to protect?** Both studies that tested moderation found nothing: South Australia across socioeconomic status, distress and life satisfaction [1], SMART Schools across sex, ethnicity, year group and school deprivation [6]. That is two nulls, from two countries, in two designs — suggestive, not settled.

**What would a real cyberbullying test look like?** South Australia collected online/offline bullying and analysed it combined [1]; Spain used official reports [1]. A pupil-reported, online-specific measure with a pre-ban baseline and a comparison group has not been run.

**How much does enforcement explain?** No study separates the effect of the rule from the effect of announcing it, training staff, and changing school culture, all of which arrive together. And the SMART Schools sensitivity analysis on the four schools where phones were genuinely inaccessible [6] is too small to answer the question it was designed for.

**Coverage note.** The evidence here rests on a small number of studies — three carry most of the weight: SMART Schools [6], the South Australian natural experiment [1], and Saffer's NBER analysis [4]. Beland and Murphy [2] and the Campbell and Edwards review [3] are cited through the authors' own plain-language summaries rather than the primary papers, which is a weaker footing than the rest and should be checked against the originals before quotation elsewhere. They are also not independent of [1]: all three are read here through the same family of open-access summaries, and [1] discusses the other two. Treat any agreement among [1], [2] and [3] as one body of testimony, not three. The Spanish bullying result is likewise second-hand [1], and the Spanish working papers were not read in this pass.

**A record note.** The upload *Sensory Syncrasis Evidence Base: Screens (Paper A) and ADHD (Paper B)* is filed under McLuhan & media theory, but its content is a screens-and-ADHD evidence review and would be found by anyone searching that topic only if the topic were broader.
