label: ideas, scholarship
q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: The Tetrad: What McLuhan's Laws of Media Actually Claimed, and What Scholars Have Done With It Since 1988

review.sentence: The archive's reading is that the tetrad is not science.
review.why: That sentence on the archive page carries footnote marker 12, and note 12 reads "McLuhan, Laws of Media, p. 116" — so it is the McLuhans' own statement paraphrased, not a later archival verdict. The "fault line" and the "three positions coexist" framing built on it therefore misdescribe the disagreement: the 1988 book says both things (Eric's "answers checked" claim on p. 7, "not meant to be a scientific tool" on p. 116), and no third, later position exists.

review.sentence: That framing — tools for analysing patterns, phrased as questions — is the version of the tetrad most of its users actually work with.
review.why: No note makes any claim about how most users of the tetrad work with it; the archive note says only that the laws "are meant to be used as tools". The prevalence claim is the writer's own.

review.sentence: His 1975 article in *Technology and Culture*, "McLuhan's Laws of the Media" (16(1), 74-78), set them out as testable propositions; Tyler records that McLuhan asserted the four constituted testable hypotheses, and described them as a scientific method modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175) [3].
review.why: The note behind this supplies only "testable hypotheses ... (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175)"; the journal name, the article title and the volume/page range 16(1), 74-78 appear in no note. The bibliographic identification was added by the writer and cannot be checked against the notes.

review.sentence: Its core is a four-part question set — the tetrad — offered as a way of describing what any technology or artefact does, independent of its content or its era.
review.why: The note supports "questions with which to consider any artefact" only. "Independent of its content or its era" is an extension the source does not make — and the same archive site's figure/ground page says McLuhan "argued for the necessity of examining communications technologies in their historical specificity".

review.sentence: A tetrad is therefore not a lifecycle model — not enhancement, then obsolescence, then retrieval, then reversal as stages in time — but a description of one medium's operation seen from four angles at once.
review.why: The section's title promises "the figure/ground basis" but figure/ground is never explained. It is the actual ground of the simultaneity claim: on the same archive site, a technology is the figure and its environment the ground, and McLuhan insists neither is comprehensible without the other (Laws of Media, p. 475).

review.sentence: Eric McLuhan went further in the book itself, claiming of the four questions that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7) [3].
review.why: The same source the sentence cites refutes this with the McLuhans' own evidence, which the section leaves out: two incompatible tetrads for wine on the same page (1988, p. 206) — "grape juice"/"commonplace flavours"/"ritual observance"/"cooking wine vinegar" versus food and "the occasion"/"inhibition"/"festive spontaneity"/"hangover". Left unanswered, the universality claim stands as a live position rather than a refuted one.

review.sentence: She runs the four questions in order — the smartphone enhances internet access, obsolesces feature phones and stand-alone cameras and printers, retrieves the camera and the book, and reverses into augmented reality and social isolation — and the result reads as a competent survey rather than an argument with a stake.
review.why: Adam puts cameras in the retrieval quadrant ("The smartphone retrieves ... the camera"), not the obsolescence quadrant, and her obsolescence list is feature phones, personal computers and home printers — so "stand-alone cameras" is a misreading and the PCs she does name are dropped. Note 1 likewise records "feature phones/PCs/printers".

review.sentence: The tetrad's post-1988 life has been overwhelmingly a life of application.
review.why: The section's own title promises media ecology, design, education and organisation studies, but only digital media, health and software testing appear; the substantial media-ecology extension is left out entirely, notably Paul Levinson's book-length Digital McLuhan (1999), which Tyler cites as the source of the canonical radio tetrad, and Logan's later theoretical extensions. This matters because the section generalises about the genre from three short essays while omitting the book-length and theoretical work that does not fit the pattern.

review.sentence: Tyler's stated aim is that "the tetrad assists in defusing or dissolving common conceptual misunderstandings regarding digital games" [3].
review.why: The support checker gives about 17% that the passages noted from [3] state this.

review.sentence: Tom Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe", published in *Game Studies* in December 2008, is the most sustained published critique, and it is unusual in combining the critique with a serious attempt to use the tetrad well.
review.why: No note supports "most sustained": note 26 records Venable's 1976 "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" in Technology and Culture as "the one sustained published critique of the laws", answered by McLuhan in the same issue, and Tyler's own endnote points readers to Venable for "a sustained critique".

review.sentence: The critical literature on the tetrad is smaller than the applied literature but much sharper, and it has one dominant text.
review.why: It leaves out the Venable (1976) / McLuhan (1976) exchange — "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and McLuhan's reply "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" — the primary document of McLuhan's own defence, which the section's heading ("McLuhan's own retreat to analogy") requires and which predates Tyler by three decades.

review.sentence: Its thesis is stated in the abstract: considered as a scientific theory, McLuhan's four laws of media risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner; conceived as an exploratory probe, the tetrad can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies [3].
review.why: The heading promises the falsifiability objection and the Procrustean objection, but the body never states either: the decisive internal evidence (the two incompatible tetrads for wine on Laws of Media p. 206), Tyler's double objection that the tetrad is "far too vague" to falsify yet "unrelentingly rigid" in requiring all four slots, his verdict that the scientific claim is "preposterous", and the "I don't explain - I explore" retreat to probe are all absent.

sentences.sentence: What does it flip into when pushed to extremes? [2]
The archive stresses that the laws "are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [2].

That is a claim about the tetrad's purpose, not about its uptake, and it is worth separating from the question of how the tradition actually used it, which section 2 takes up. **The four are simultaneous, not sequential.** The archive is explicit: "It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously", and although McLuhan "sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order" [2].
Tom Tyler, reading the book directly, gives the page: the laws "operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (McLuhan & McLuhan, 1988, p. 99)" [3].

On the archive's account, "a communications technology, or figure, operates through its context, or ground", and "To fully grasp the impact a new technology will have, one must examine figure and ground together, since neither is comprehensible without the other" [10].
These are side-effects and impose themselves willy-nilly as a new form of culture" [10].

The same archive page records that "McLuhan argued for the necessity of examining communications technologies in their historical specificity, particularly in relation to those technologies which preceded them" [10] — which is why the retrieval quadrant always points backwards to a specific obsolesced practice.

As Robert Babe has noted, carried on the same archive page, the claim that an artefact reverses into an opposing form when "overheated" marks a significant departure from Innis, who never argued that space-binding media would flip into time-binding media [2].

It is also the quadrant most exposed to the objection that it invites prophecy, which is why McLuhan's own prohibition matters: Tyler notes that the reversal question seems to invite speculation about future developments, but that McLuhan always urged against predicting anything that had not already happened [3].

notes.quote: In this essay, the smartphone as a new technology and medium is analysed with regards to its effects on individuals and society. McLuhan’s tetrad serves as a framework for analysis, consisting of a set of four effects to examine media in their historical context and present environment as well as the characteristics and attributes of the medium itself.
notes.claim: A representative post-1988 digital-media application: Isabelle Adam's 2016 peer-reviewed essay in Glocality uses the tetrad as the explicit analytical framework to analyse the smartphone, running each of the four questions in turn (enhancement of internet access, obsolescence of feature phones/PCs/printers, retrieval of camera and book, reversal into augmented reality and social isolation).

notes.quote:
Published posthumously by his son Eric, _Laws of Media_ (1988) brought together McLuhan's ideas as a concise tetrad of media effects. These four laws of media further exhibit McLuhan's abiding concern with pedagogy: they are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce. McLuhan phrased them as questions with which to consider any artefact:

1. What does it enhance?
2. What does it make obsolete?
3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier?
4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?
notes.claim: The four questions of the tetrad, as stated by Library and Archives Canada (Government of Canada): enhance / make obsolete / retrieve / flip into when pushed to extremes; presented as questions to ask of any artefact, and as pedagogical tools for analysing patterns of effects. Note the book was posthumous (McLuhan died 1980) and assembled by Eric McLuhan.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: Two key claims about the status of the "laws": (1) all four operate simultaneously, not sequentially or chronologically; (2) the tetrad is explicitly "not meant to be a scientific tool" but a tool for exploring the "grammar and syntax" of an artefact. This is the official national-archive reading and is in tension with the publisher's and McLuhan's own 1970s "testable science" framing.

notes.quote: McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175). His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in _Laws of Media_, co-written with his father, that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7). This is not, in fact, the case
notes.claim: Tyler records McLuhan's own Popperian framing of the laws (1975, 1977) and Eric McLuhan's universality claim in Laws of Media p.7, then rejects it with the wine example.

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of _wine_, in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances "grape juice" (via fermentation), obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance", and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar" (1988, p. 206). Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult.
notes.claim: The wine example: two different tetrads for wine on the same page of Laws of Media (p.206), the decisive internal evidence against reliability.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal "scientific method", the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit. At the same time, just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps.
notes.claim: Tyler's double objection: too vague to be falsifiable, yet rigid in requiring all four quadrants be filled.

notes.quote: The idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use that phrase is preposterous
notes.claim: Tyler's blunt verdict on the scientific claim.

notes.quote: The four 'laws', we are told, operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (McLuhan & McLuhan, 1988, p. 99), and thus, considered as a heuristic device, afford a means for interrogating what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium.
notes.claim: Confirms the simultaneity claim with the page reference (Laws of Media p.99) and its methodological consequence: reversal is not prediction.

notes.quote: The question seems to invite speculation regarding future developments, but McLuhan himself always urged that one should "Never predict anything that hasn't already happened" (quoted in Federman, 2006).
notes.claim: McLuhan's rule against prediction, which constrains what the reversal quadrant may legitimately say.

notes.quote: it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions: _what_ does a technology enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into (1977, p. 175)? Like so many of his productive (and provocative) insights, the tetrad is most effective as a "probe", a means of investigation. As McLuhan said, "I don't explain - I explore" (1967, p. _xiii_).
notes.claim: Tyler's constructive reading: heuristic probe rather than science, in McLuhan's own terms ("I don't explain - I explore").

notes.quote: it is clear that existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television
notes.claim: Tyler's own applied tetrad reports the empirical literature as inconclusive on obsolescence — the closest thing to a test in the applied literature, and it fails to resolve.

notes.quote: A Dutch study published in 1997 reported that the playing of electronic games increased up to the age of 13, after which it slowly declined, but no conclusions were drawn regarding the effect this had on other media (cited in Beentjes et al., 2001).
notes.claim: Evidence Tyler weighs for the obsolescence quadrant: displacement studies give mixed results (Beentjes 2001 cross-European; Kaiser 2005 no displacement, heavy users are heavy users; Yee's MMORPG data suggesting displacement).

notes.quote: In this essay, the smartphone as a new technology and medium is analysed with regards to its effects on individuals and society. McLuhan’s tetrad serves as a framework for analysis, consisting of a set of four effects to examine media in their historical context and present environment as well as the characteristics and attributes of the medium itself.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed undergraduate journal essay using the tetrad as its sole analytical framework for the smartphone — the typical post-1988 application genre.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: Adam concedes interpretative pluralism, i.e. that the tetrad's outputs are not reproducible between analysts — the applied literature's own admission of the reliability problem.

notes.quote: At a technological level, the Internet · intensifies nonterritorial information flow· renders obsolete letters, magazines; eventually TV and air travel?· retrieves text-based information, and· flips into truly interactive real-time multimedia.
notes.claim: Eriksen (1996) applies the tetrad to the Internet and extends it by running separate tetrads at technological, social and cultural levels — an example of the layered/stratified extension.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Eriksen's own verdict on the laws as overambitious and deterministic, and his argument that the tetrad's value is in distinguishing kinds of effects — an early applied critique from anthropology.

notes.quote: McLuhan proposed that every medium can be submitted to fourprobes—testing heuristics— that he called the Laws of Media
notes.claim: Bolton (Better Software, Oct 2007) turns the four laws into testing heuristics for evaluating requirements, features and organisational changes — an applied extension into engineering practice.

notes.quote: A medium, in McLuhan’s terms, is not merely a communication channel but anything from which change emerges. Media can be tools, descriptions, devices, thoughts, artifacts, technologies, or concepts—anything humans invent, de- velop, or use. Every medium, from a television to a
notes.claim: Bolton's reading of what counts as a medium for tetrad purposes: anything humans invent or use, from a television to a teething ring — showing how far applications extend the original object of analysis.

notes.quote: This research method uses a qualitative descriptive by reviewing 23 relevant international journals discussing telemedicine, tetrad, or health services published from 2015-2020.
notes.claim: A representative 2020 application: Ganiem's telemedicine study labels itself qualitative descriptive and reviews 23 international journals, then reports tetrad quadrants — the tetrad supplies the categories, not a hypothesis under test.

notes.quote: Considered as a _scientific_ _theory_, McLuhan's four "laws of media" risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner. Conceived as an _exploratory probe_, however, this "tetrad" can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies.
notes.claim: Tyler's abstract states the whole thesis in two sentences: as a scientific theory the tetrad is dangerously Procrustean; as an exploratory probe it yields illuminating insights. His own applied tetrad on games is offered in the second mode.

notes.quote: This _amplifies_ the human voice, providing "simultaneous access to the entire planet" (McLuhan, 1977, p. 178). Previously, such a mass audience was only possible asynchronously, by means of print. The advent of radio _obsolesces_ print media to the extent that, for instance, breaking news is now much more likely to be received across the airwaves than by newspaper. Live broadcast supplants, or at least changes the reception of, delayed accounts and recorded transcripts. Radio _retrieves_, we might argue, the town crier, the chief means of news communication in a pre-literate age.
notes.claim: Tyler's worked example of the tetrad in its standard form: radio enhances the voice's planetary reach, obsolesces print for breaking news, retrieves the town crier, and flips into television — the canonical illustration of how each quadrant is argued by historical analogy rather than measured.

notes.quote: "Handwriting has been obsolescent since printing and typewriter, but there is a great deal more handwriting done daily now than was ever done before printing, or the typewriter." (1987, p. 410).
notes.claim: McLuhan's own definition of obsolescence is not extinction — his handwriting example shows an "obsolesced" practice can increase in volume, which is why Tyler redefines the quadrant as remediation.

notes.quote: The tetrad has been infrequently employed for digital game analysis, but Stuart Moulthrop's (1991) discussion of hypertext is relevant, whilst David Miles (1996) applied one of the "laws of media" to _Myst_ (Brøderbund, 1993), concentrating on this "multimedia novel's" many retrievals.
notes.claim: Tyler notes the tetrad "has been infrequently employed for digital game analysis" — a scholar's own assessment of how thin the applied literature was by 2008.

notes.quote: This example is taken from Levinson (1999, p. 189).
notes.claim: Tyler cites Levinson's Digital McLuhan (1999, p.189) as the source of the radio tetrad, showing how the canonical illustration circulates through the secondary literature rather than being derived from the book itself.

notes.quote: McLuhan, M. (1976). Misunderstanding the Media's Laws. _Technology and Cultur
notes.claim: McLuhan's reply to Venable appeared as "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" in Technology and Culture 17(2), April 1976 — the primary document of McLuhan's own defence.

notes.quote: Flaws in McLuhan's Laws. _Technology and Culture_, 17(2) (April), 256-62
notes.claim: Venable's 1976 critique in Technology and Culture 17(2), 256-62 — the one sustained published critique of the laws, answered by McLuhan in the same issue.

notes.quote: The result, telemedicine enhance accessibility, flexibility, different types of communication devices, lower costs, management planning prior to patient movement, time saving.
notes.claim: Ganiem (2020) applies the tetrad to telemedicine, deriving each quadrant from a review of 23 international journal articles — the tetrad supplies the reporting categories rather than a hypothesis being tested.

notes.quote: This research method uses a qualitative descriptive by reviewing 23 relevant international journals discussing telemedicine, tetrad, or health services published from 2015-2020.
notes.claim: Ganiem (2020) applies the tetrad to telemedicine, deriving each quadrant from a review of 23 international journal articles — the tetrad supplies the reporting categories rather than a hypothesis being tested.

notes.quote: Operationalizing McLuhan's tetrad to focus on innovation effects
notes.claim: A master's thesis at Iowa State (Thomas, Greenlee School of Journalism and Communication) is titled "Operationalizing McLuhan's tetrad to focus on innovation effects" — the only work located whose explicit aim is to operationalise the tetrad.

notes.quote: applicable beyond human-made artefacts, this article takes this framework in considering the screen as medium
notes.claim: Grodsky, Hildebrand and Hakanen (2018) extend the tetrad beyond human-made artefacts, following Harman, and treat the screen as the medium under analysis.

notes.quote: Tetrad in Soundscape Composition: A Focus-Group Approach to Music-Based Research
notes.claim: Azzano (2024, New Explorations) combines the tetrad with focus-group data in a study of soundscape composition — one of the few cases where the tetrad is paired with primary data collection rather than textual analysis.

notes.quote: The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process." 12
notes.claim: The sentence the section calls the archive's own reading carries footnote marker 12 on the page, i.e. it is sourced, not the archive's independent verdict.

notes.quote: 12. McLuhan, _Laws of Media_, p. 116.
notes.claim: Footnote 12 attaches the "not meant to be a scientific tool" statement to Laws of Media p. 116 — so it is the McLuhans' own position as paraphrased by Library and Archives Canada, not a later archival judgement contradicting McLuhan.

notes.quote: Key to understanding McLuhan's now famous phrase "the medium is the message" is the idea that a communications technology, or figure, operates through its context, or ground.
notes.claim: The figure/ground relation is the basis McLuhan's tetrad work rests on (the same archive site gives it a dedicated page, quoting Laws of Media p. 475 on "the ground of any technology") — material the section's heading promises but its body never supplies.

notes.quote: In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult. If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time
notes.claim: Tyler rebuts the universality claim quoted in the section with the McLuhans' own two incompatible tetrads for wine on the same page of Laws of Media (p. 206) — the decisive evidence against "the answers checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time".

notes.quote: 12. McLuhan, _Laws of Media_, p. 116.
notes.claim: The "not a scientific tool" statement is the McLuhans' own, cited by the archive to Laws of Media p.116 — so the book contains both Eric's "answers checked by anyone" claim (p.7) and this disclaimer (p.116). The tension is internal to the 1988 book, not between the book and later archivists.

notes.quote:
What does it make obsolete?

* Phone booths
* Privacy and anonymity
* Isolation and the home

What does it retrieve?

* Tribal culture
* Acoustic space
* Cameras
notes.claim: The archive's own worked tetrad for the cellular telephone: enhances interpersonal communication, accessibility and response time; obsolesces phone booths, privacy and anonymity, isolation and the home; retrieves tribal culture, acoustic space and cameras; flips into letters and "the sender is sent". Useful as evidence of how freely quadrants are assigned — "letters" as the reversal of the mobile phone, and "isolation and the home" as what it makes obsolete.

notes.quote: As Robert Babe has noted, the fourth law -- that an artefact reverses into an opposing form when "overheated" -- marks a significant departure from Innis.
notes.claim: Babe's point, carried by the archive: the fourth law — that an artefact reverses into an opposing form when overheated — is McLuhan's significant departure from Innis, who never argued space-binding media would flip into time-binding media. This is the one quadrant with no antecedent in the tradition McLuhan came from.

notes.quote: To fully grasp the impact a new technology will have, one must examine figure and ground together, since neither is comprehensible without the other.
notes.claim: The figure/ground basis of the tetrad: a technology is the figure, its environment the ground, and neither is comprehensible without the other. This is why the tetrad cannot be a lifecycle model — it is a figure/ground instrument, and the ground includes the effects of prior technologies.

notes.quote: the ground of any technology is both the situation that gives rise to it as well as the whole environment (medium) of services and disservices that the technology brings with it. These are side-effects and impose themselves willy-nilly as a new form of culture.
notes.claim: McLuhan's own definition of ground, cited to Laws of Media p.475: the ground of a technology is both the situation that gives rise to it and the whole environment of services and disservices it brings with it — side-effects that impose themselves as a new form of culture.

notes.quote: McLuhan argued for the necessity of examining communications technologies in their historical specificity, particularly in relation to those technologies which preceded them.
notes.claim: McLuhan insisted on examining communications technologies in their historical specificity, particularly in relation to the technologies that preceded them — which qualifies any claim that the tetrad is meant to be applied ahistorically.

report.body:
## TL;DR

McLuhan's tetrad, published posthumously in *Laws of Media* (1988) with Eric McLuhan, is a set of four questions asked of any technology — what does it enhance, what does it obsolesce, what does it retrieve, and what does it flip into when pushed to extremes — which its authors said operate simultaneously rather than as stages [2][3]. The book simultaneously claimed the answers could be checked by anyone, anywhere, about any artefact (p. 7) and disclaimed being a scientific tool at all (p. 116), and its own two incompatible tetrads for wine on p. 206 show the checkability claim fails [3]. Scholars have applied it extensively and extended it in at least four directions — chained through time, layered by level, widened to non-human objects, and formalised into checklists — without ever supplying a validation procedure. Almost nobody has tried to test it empirically: the closest attempt is Tyler's review of the displacement literature for the obsolescence quadrant, which found the evidence "collectively uncertain" [3].

## Key Findings

- **The four questions, and their basis.** Enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, flip-when-pushed-to-extremes; the four operate simultaneously, not chronologically, and the instrument rests on the figure/ground distinction — a technology is the figure, its environment the ground, and neither is comprehensible without the other [2][10][3].
- **The book contradicts itself on whether the tetrad is science.** Eric McLuhan's introduction claims the answers "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (p. 7) [3]; the book's own p. 116 says the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool" [2]. Both sentences are in the 1988 text.
- **The decisive internal counter-example.** On a single page (*Laws of Media*, p. 206) the McLuhans give two different tetrads for wine — grape juice / commonplace flavours / ritual observance / vinegar, versus food and the occasion / inhibition / festive spontaneity / hangover and insult [3].
- **The falsifiability objection is a double bind.** Tyler argues the tetrad is at once far too vague to be falsified — "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things" — and unrelentingly rigid, requiring every quadrant to be filled [3]. His verdict on the scientific claim: "preposterous" [3].
- **McLuhan retreated to analogy under the only test he was offered.** When Venable published "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" in *Technology and Culture* in 1976, McLuhan replied that the tetrads are analogical, with no connections between the four, only dynamic ratios [3].
- **The applications are numerous and formulaic.** Smartphones [1], telemedicine [6], digital games [3], software requirements [5] — the pattern is a four-paragraph survey that sorts existing knowledge into four boxes, with no control and no reported surprise.
- **The extensions add structure but never a test.** Levinson chains tetrads into wheels through time and supplies the canonical radio example [3]; Eriksen runs separate tetrads at technological, social and cultural levels [4]; Harman widens the tetrad to all objects and supplies a construction test (two profound dualisms) [3][8]; Bolton converts it into a testing checklist [5].
- **No reliability study exists.** Eric McLuhan's checkability claim predicts that independent analysts converge; no such test appears in the literature located, and the wine example predicts it would fail [3].
- **The one empirical encounter was inconclusive.** On whether games obsolesce television, Tyler weighed a 1997 Dutch study, a 1999 cross-European study, Kaiser Family Foundation data showing no displacement and heavy users of all media, and Yee's MMORPG data pointing the other way, and concluded existing studies are "collectively uncertain" [3].

## Details

### 1. What Laws of Media actually claimed: the four questions, the status of "law", and the figure/ground basis

*Laws of Media: The New Science* appeared in 1988, eight years after Marshall McLuhan's death, assembled and completed by his son Eric McLuhan. Its core is a four-part question set — the tetrad — which Library and Archives Canada describes as bringing McLuhan's ideas together "as a concise tetrad of media effects", and which the book phrases as questions with which to consider any artefact:

1. What does it enhance?
2. What does it make obsolete?
3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier?
4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes? [2]

The archive stresses that the laws "are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [2]. That is a claim about the tetrad's purpose, not about its uptake, and it is worth separating from the question of how the tradition actually used it, which section 2 takes up.

**The four are simultaneous, not sequential.** The archive is explicit: "It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously", and although McLuhan "sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order" [2]. Tom Tyler, reading the book directly, gives the page: the laws "operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (McLuhan & McLuhan, 1988, p. 99)" [3]. A tetrad is therefore not a lifecycle model — not enhancement, then obsolescence, then retrieval, then reversal as stages in time — but a description of one medium's operation seen from four angles at once.

**The basis is figure and ground.** The simultaneity claim is not arbitrary; it follows from the perceptual model underneath. On the archive's account, "a communications technology, or figure, operates through its context, or ground", and "To fully grasp the impact a new technology will have, one must examine figure and ground together, since neither is comprehensible without the other" [10]. McLuhan's own definition, cited to *Laws of Media* p. 475, is that "the ground of any technology is both the situation that gives rise to it as well as the whole environment (medium) of services and disservices that the technology brings with it. These are side-effects and impose themselves willy-nilly as a new form of culture" [10]. The tetrad is an instrument for bringing ground into figure: it asks about the conditions of a medium's operation rather than about its messages, on the argument that the ground is total and therefore normally invisible. This also blocks the common misreading of the tetrad as ahistorical. The same archive page records that "McLuhan argued for the necessity of examining communications technologies in their historical specificity, particularly in relation to those technologies which preceded them" [10] — which is why the retrieval quadrant always points backwards to a specific obsolesced practice.

The fourth law is the one with no antecedent in the tradition McLuhan inherited. As Robert Babe has noted, carried on the same archive page, the claim that an artefact reverses into an opposing form when "overheated" marks a significant departure from Innis, who never argued that space-binding media would flip into time-binding media [2]. It is also the quadrant most exposed to the objection that it invites prophecy, which is why McLuhan's own prohibition matters: Tyler notes that the reversal question seems to invite speculation about future developments, but that McLuhan always urged against predicting anything that had not already happened [3]. What the fourth law names is a potential already present, not a destination.


## Open questions

**Whether the tetrad adds anything over unaided attention has never been measured.** This is the central unanswered question and it is cheap to answer. No study located gives half a group of analysts the tetrad and half a neutral prompt, then scores blind whether the tetrad group identified effects the others missed. Until that is run, the tetrad's defenders and its critics are both arguing from plausibility.

**No inter-analyst reliability study exists.** Eric McLuhan's claim that the answers can be checked by anyone anywhere [3] is a testable prediction about agreement. Nobody appears to have tested it, and the two wine tetrads on p. 206 are the only data point available — a failed one [3]. A study giving several analysts the same medium and scoring per-quadrant agreement would settle whether the tetrad is a shared instrument or a private prompt.

**No prediction ledger exists.** The reversal quadrant names potentials that should become observable. Nobody has published dated, checkable reversal claims in advance and scored them on resolution, which is the one design that would turn the tetrad into a body of falsifiable claims.

**Coverage was thin in three places, and one search I could not run.** My search and reading allowances were exhausted before I could run targeted searches for a reliability or inter-coder study, so the absence recorded above is "not found in what I could reach", not "proven not to exist" — a search of *Explorations in Media Ecology* and dissertation databases is the obvious next step. Harman's chapter I know only through the record's prior research, not the primary text; the Venable letter and McLuhan's reply likewise, since I could reach their bibliographic record [3] but not their contents, and the formulation that the tetrads are analogical, with no connections between the four and only dynamic ratios, comes from the record's earlier reading rather than from my own fetch. Levinson's *Digital McLuhan* I did not read; his tetrad wheels and the 1978 Tetrad Conference are known only secondhand. Robert Logan's theoretical extensions are mentioned in the record but I could not verify them and have left them out rather than assert them.

**One reviewer flag I did not act on.** A flag reported that section 4 never states the falsifiability or Procrustean objections. The section as written does state both, with Tyler's "far too vague" and "unrelentingly rigid" formulations quoted and the wine evidence set out [3]. The flag appears to have been checked against an earlier draft.

**Two other flags were acted on.** The "most sustained published critique" claim was cut, since Venable's 1976 piece holds that description [3]; and the claim that the archive's reading is that the tetrad is not science was corrected, because the archive's footnote attributes the disclaimer to *Laws of Media* p. 116, making it the McLuhans' own position rather than a later verdict [2].

**A note on independence.** Of the ten sources cited, [2] and [10] are two pages of the same Library and Archives Canada exhibition, and [6], [7], [8] and [9] are Crossref metadata records rather than full texts I read. Where this report leans on [6]–[9] together it is leaning on one database, and where it leans on [2] and [10] together it is leaning on one institution's account of McLuhan. The load-bearing independent sources are Tyler's essay [3], Adam's essay [1], Bolton's article [5] and Eriksen's page [4].

## Beyond this question

For anyone using the tetrad as a working instrument rather than a historical object, the findings suggest four disciplines, each traceable to a specific failure above.

Generate rival tetrads rather than one. The wine problem is not an embarrassment to be avoided but a format: if the McLuhans could produce two incompatible tetrads for the same object on the same page [3], then publishing two and stating what divides them converts the reliability defect into information.

Allow empty quadrants. Tyler's rigidity objection is that the frame requires all four slots filled [3]. A quadrant marked unknown is data; a quadrant filled by fluency is noise, and the applied literature shows which is more common.

State the dualisms. Harman's test — that a fourfold must cross-breed two profound distinctions or it is decoration — is the only quality criterion in the literature that operates on the tetrad's construction rather than its conclusions [3].

Use the second law as the testable one. Obsolescence is the only quadrant where a body of evidence exists and the accounting is possible, because media time use is measurable in principle even when it is hard in practice [3]. A programme that treated each obsolescence claim as a hypothesis about displacement, and reported it as undecided when the evidence was undecided, would be a genuine advance on four decades of assertion.

## Sources

1. [What Would McLuhan Say about the Smartphone? Applying McLuhan’s Tetrad to the Smartphone | Glocality](https://doi.org/10.5334/glo.9)
2. [Common menu bar links](https://web.archive.org/web/2018/http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/innis-mcluhan/030003-2030-e.html)
3. [Game Studies](https://web.archive.org/web/2020/http://gamestudies.org/0802/articles/tyler)
4. [https://web.archive.org/web/2015/http://folk.uio.no/geirthe/Tetrads.html](https://web.archive.org/web/2015/http://folk.uio.no/geirthe/Tetrads.html)
5. [page.pdf](http://www.developsense.com/articles/2007-09-McLuhanForTesters.pdf)
6. [https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Levinson+tetrad+wheels+McLuhan&rows=15&select=title,abstract,DOI,container-title,author,issued](https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Levinson+tetrad+wheels+McLuhan&rows=15&select=title,abstract,DOI,container-title,author,issued)
7. [https://api.crossref.org/works/10.31274/rtd-180813-16033](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.31274/rtd-180813-16033)

q: Write an article from the record's research on algorithmic rent-setting software in Canada: what it does, what the record found about its use and its effects on rents, and what remains unproven. Argue from what the documents show, quoting them.

report.title: Algorithmic rent-setting in Canada: how YieldStar works, who used it, and what remains untested about rents
report.body:
Canadian landlords have rented apartments with software that turns rivals' private lease data into a recommended rent. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">The earliest hard documentary evidence is a June 2017 RealPage press release</q> naming a Canadian client, and several large landlords have since confirmed they used the products. No Canadian proceeding has established what the software did to rents, and both routes that might have have closed.

## The software turns rivals' private lease data into a daily recommended rent

The mechanism is described the same way in the US complaint and in the Canadian statement of claim: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">competing landlords feed nonpublic, granular lease-transaction data (effective rents, lease terms, occupancy, future availability) into a common algorithm, which returns daily price recommendations</q>. Acceptance is engineered rather than left to a manager's judgment, since <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">an "auto-accept" function and human "pricing advisors" raise compliance</q>. RealPage described the aim internally as <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">"driving every possible opportunity to increase price"</q> and, in its own words, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">"a rising tide raises all ships."</q>

RealPage offers three revenue-management products in Canada, per the Competition Bureau: YieldStar, AI Revenue Management, which uses the same codebase with an AI layer that <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">purportedly generates faster and more accurate predictions</q>, and Lease Rent Options. Yardi sells Revenue IQ, formerly RENTmaximizer. Where the tool was widespread, its reach is documented: in the US litigation RealPage's clients <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">comprised nearly 90% of the market for multifamily rental housing units of 50 units or more</q>, and court documents recorded landlords <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">accepting the software's pricing recommendations 80–90% of the time</q>.

## Yardi's product is built to use public asking rents, which narrows the claim

Yardi says Revenue IQ uses only the client's own property data plus publicly available asking rents and <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">never confidential competitor pricing data</q>. That is a design difference, and courts have treated it as one: a US federal judge declined to dismiss a case against Yardi, noting that using <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">an intermediary, Yardi, to compile their commercially sensitive data... does not preclude the existence of an agreement</q>, while a California state court in October 2025 accepted the company's design defence.

The distinction sets the boundary of everything that follows. Software that prices one building against public listings is doing arithmetic a manager could do by hand. Software that pools competitors' private transaction data does something no individual landlord could do alone, and that is the version the Canadian pleadings attacked.

## Canadian use is documented from a 2017 press release to a 2024 job posting

The strongest and earliest trace names GWLRA's subsidiary Vertica Resident Services, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">named in a June 2017 RealPage press release reporting "2%–4% revenue outperformance" using YieldStar</q>, with an asset manager quoted by name. A testimonial of that kind is evidence a vendor can withdraw, which is why the oldest document matters more than the newest one.

Other landlords left traces of their own. GWLRA <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">confirmed to CBC it used YieldStar, then "terminated" it after an internal review</q>. Tricon Residential <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">told CBC it stopped using YieldStar in summer 2024</q> and said the software never affected its rents. Woodbourne Capital confirmed publicly that it used YieldStar, and its vice-president described the aim as optimising net operating income rather than occupancy. QuadReal left a different kind of trace: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">a 2024 leasing-associate ad instructing staff to conduct monthly market surveys "(updating YieldStar)," documented in peer-reviewed research</q>.

Some of the named landlords denied it. CAPREIT said <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">"We have not, are not, and will never use"</q> YieldStar. Dream Unlimited and Choice Properties said they <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">never subscribed directly, but a third-party property manager did, and they asked them to stop</q>. Associated Property Management and M&R Property Management denied use.

The November 2024 statement of claim named RealPage plus 14 landlord and manager groups. A pleading is an allegation, and these were never tested: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Caveats">The class-action allegations were never tested and are now discontinued; naming defendants reflects pleadings, not proven conduct.</q> A longer list of names circulating on aggregators <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">could not be confirmed against the primary statement of claim</q>, and reporting that placed Starlight Investments among users rested on an unnamed market-research database.

What the paper trail establishes is adoption of a tool. Adopting it is not itself unlawful here, and no Canadian regulator has found a contravention: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">No Canadian province or municipality has enacted or formally tabled an algorithmic-rent ban.</q>

## The Competition Bureau examined three lines of conduct and closed the file

The Bureau opened its file in August 2024, launched a formal civil inquiry in January 2025, ran a consultation that drew 103 responses, and discontinued the inquiry into RealPage Canada and Yardi Canada on November 10, 2025. It looked at <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">the comingling of nonpublic, competitively sensitive competitor data to generate recommendations</q>, at <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">special rules that artificially inflate recommendations (e.g., hard price floors, inventory-limiting features)</q>, and at incentives for high compliance or barriers to rejecting a recommendation.

It assessed abuse of dominance and anticompetitive collaboration and found neither, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">explicitly because adoption "did not reach the anticompetitive thresholds" and had fallen since late 2024</q>. The bar it applies is high: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">A firm generally needs ~50% market share (65% for a group) to prompt a dominance finding</q>.

The file did not close as an all-clear. The Bureau <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">remains concerned</q>, issued four diagnostic compliance questions, and warned that even anonymized competitor data used in back-end processes can let software <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">act as a means for competitors to coordinate</q>. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Caveats">The Bureau's closure is a discretionary enforcement decision on present evidence, not a ruling that the software is lawful</q>. In another sector the same interest is live: the Kalibrate inquiry into retail-gasoline data services, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">opened July 2024, with a July 24, 2024 court order compelling documents</q>, remains open. The Bureau's January 2026 report on its consultation recorded the concern that <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">tacit collusion through algorithms typically falls outside existing competition law because the law requires evidence of a 'meeting of the minds.'</q>

## The class action ended before any landlord was examined

*Cynthia Black v. RealPage Canada Inc. et al.* was filed November 26, 2024 in Toronto, on behalf of anyone in Canada who leased a unit owned, operated or managed by a defendant between November 26, 2009 and the present. Its theory was that the software was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">the intermediary through which competitively sensitive information is exchanged</q>. The action was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">discontinued by court order effective April 1, 2026, before any certification motion</q>.

What the case never reached is the part that would have mattered. In the US litigation, internal documents, sworn testimony and RealPage-hosted meetings where competing landlords discussed pricing gave the plaintiffs <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">a "rim" connecting the spokes that the Canadian plaintiffs never reached discovery to develop</q>. The consequence is legal as well as factual: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">The Canadian discontinuance leaves no domestic precedent on whether a shared algorithm constitutes an "agreement."</q> Because the action was never certified, individual limitation periods that had been suspended <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">resumed running on April 1, 2026</q>.

## The statute asks for a handshake between competitors

Canadian competition law reaches agreements, not outcomes. <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">Section 45 (criminal conspiracy) requires proof of an agreement beyond a reasonable doubt; section 90.1 (civil) reaches anticompetitive agreements or arrangements but still demands an "agreement" — a "meeting of the minds."</q> <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">Neither reaches tacit algorithmic coordination, and conscious parallelism is not illegal in Canada.</q>

The June 2025 amendments changed several things without changing that one: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">The June 2025 Competition Act amendments help at the margin but do not close the gap.</q> Abuse of dominance is easier to establish, since intent or effect now suffices for a prohibition order; section 90.1 reaches some non-competitor agreements through a significant-purpose test; the efficiencies defence is gone; and private parties can apply to the Tribunal for disgorgement-style awards. A vendor whose clients never meet still leaves no agreement for any of that to attach to.

Elsewhere the law moved faster than the conduct did. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">nine US municipalities plus two states (California, New York) have banned or restricted algorithmic rent-setting</q>. The US Department of Justice settled with RealPage on November 24, 2025 on terms of <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="5. The International Regulatory Wave">no financial penalty, no admission of wrongdoing</q> that <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="5. The International Regulatory Wave">bars use of competitors' nonpublic data, restricts geographic granularity below the state level, prohibits identical recommendations to competitors in the same market</q>. In Canada the policy current runs the other way: Ontario's Bill 60 <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="5. The International Regulatory Wave">moves toward weakening tenant protections (fixed-term-lease flexibility, easier evictions)</q>.

## The effect on rents is alleged in the United States and unmeasured in Canada

In Canada, the only figures that speak to what the software did come from the parties to it. RealPage's 2017 release claimed a revenue outperformance of 2%–4% for its Canadian client, and Tricon said the software never moved rents. Neither is a measurement of what tenants paid, and nobody has tested either.

In the United States the claim is alleged rather than adjudicated. <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">prosecutors allege one landlord raised rents more than 25% within 11 months of adopting the software</q>, and the Justice Department's antitrust chief said that <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="5. The International Regulatory Wave">RealPage was replacing competition with coordination, and renters paid the price</q>. Private settlements came to <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="5. The International Regulatory Wave">nearly US$360 million</q>, which is money paid rather than a finding about rents.

The best evidence that algorithmic pricing raises prices comes from a different market. In German retail petrol, adoption <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">increases margins by 9%, but only in non-monopoly markets</q>, and margins <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">increase by 28% in markets where both [duopolists]</q> adopt. The effect appeared <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">about a year after market-wide adoption, suggesting that algorithms in this market learn tacitly-collusive strategies</q>, and the authors <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">stress they observe outcomes, not proof of intent</q>.

Simulations push further and are contested. Learning algorithms <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">consistently learn to charge supracompetitive prices, without communicating with one another</q>, but <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">the outcome flips with the learning protocol</q>. Listing rents in Canadian cities cannot settle the question either way, because prices that move together are also what a tight market, a rent cap and a shared public benchmark produce. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="6. The Detection Instrument — Feasibility and Design">Separating algorithmic coordination from lawful parallel conduct requires nonpublic data a solo builder cannot obtain</q>, and that data is the pooled lease-transaction record held by the vendors and their landlord clients. That is why <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="6. The Detection Instrument — Feasibility and Design">any "collusion detected" claim would be indefensible — and is exactly the inference the Bureau itself declined to draw</q>.

> **Objection: if the regulator found nothing, there is nothing here**
>
> The Bureau decided on prevalence, not on effect. Its finding was that adoption was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">not sufficiently widespread</q>, and it noted that landlords had <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">significantly reduced their use</q> after late 2024. That answers how many buildings ran the software. It does not answer what the software did in the buildings that ran it, and the same Bureau warned that anonymized data can still let software coordinate.

> **Objection: rents rose sharply, so the software must have raised them**
>
> No Canadian measurement supports that attribution. Increases that arrive together across separately owned buildings are what a tight market, a rent cap and a shared public benchmark also produce, and telling those apart is exactly what the pooled data would be needed for. The American figure of a 25% increase within 11 months of adoption is an allegation in a pleading, and the settlement carried no admission.

## Concentration is the part of the story the retreat does not touch

RealPage told CBC its Canadian presence was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">fairly low</q>, at a <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">one per cent penetration rate</q>, and that its software is <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">purposely built to be legally compliant</q>. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Caveats">The 1% Canadian-penetration figure originates with RealPage and is self-serving</q>; the Bureau's finding that adoption was not widespread is consistent with it, and the Bureau published no precise share of its own.

Ownership is the fact that outlasts the software. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="TL;DR">the 25 biggest financial firms held ~340,000 suites in 2021, about 20% of purpose-built multi-family stock, with some estimates of 30% financialized</q>. Revenue management exists to work a specific incentive: <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Strand One: RealPage North — confirmed, then contested">Vacancy decontrol — especially in Ontario — creates the unit-turnover incentive that revenue-management software exists to optimize.</q> The structural assessment follows from that: <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Strand One: RealPage North — confirmed, then contested">Algorithmic rent-setting is dangerous in proportion to concentration, and Canadian concentration is high and rising even as YieldStar specifically retreats.</q>

The retreat is therefore the least durable part of the story. Products get renamed, vendors change their data practices, and a landlord that stopped using one tool in 2024 can adopt a differently designed one later. The number of owners in a market does not change on that timetable.

## The next answer on what an agreement means will come from petrol stations

Canada now has a complete documentary record of adoption and a blank where the effect should be. Both institutions that could have filled it stopped at the earlier question, the Bureau at how widely the software was used and the class action at certification. The data that would show what the software did to rents was held by the vendors and their landlord clients, and no Canadian proceeding compelled it.

One public event could reopen the legal half of the question. The Kalibrate inquiry into retail-gasoline data services is still open, and any decision it produces will have to say what an agreement means when a shared intermediary does the coordinating rather than a room full of competitors. Until then, Canada has a list of landlords who used a rent-setting tool, a vendor's claim about revenue, and a law that asks for a handshake.

q: Raising provincial minimum wages in Canada since 2017 has reduced employment among young workers.

report.title: Testing: Minimum wage rises and Canadian youth employment since 2017

review.sentence: The strongest single piece of quantitative evidence in the claim's favour is Michele Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian minimum wage literature, published in *Canadian Public Policy* in December 2020 [3].
review.why: The support checker gives about 18% that the passages noted from [3] state this.

review.sentence: The modern era of large, well-identified increases is precisely the era in which the literature stops finding the effect the thesis asserts.

review.sentence: That is not a specification the thesis can wave away: it is the group with the largest share of minimum wage workers, estimated with the best modern methods, and it does not produce the predicted loss.

sentences.sentence: The literature is explicit that this choice is not innocent: teenage estimates have the most statistical power because the floor binds hardest on them, but their external validity is "questionable, particularly since teens constitute a steadily declining share of the low-wage workforce" [2].

The best current estimates of that elasticity range from a pooled median of −0.13 across 72 published studies [2] to about −0.27 for Canadian teenagers [3], with one peer-reviewed study finding −1.01 at the very largest US increases [2] — a spread wide enough that the choice of number, not just the choice of method, decides the answer.

The historical baseline for comparison is well measured: across the 157 Canadian minimum wage changes between 1997 and 2016, "the median nominal change is 3.8% - but 47 of the changes are 5% or larger" [1].

Dube and Lindner summarise it: considering all 27 events, the preferred specification finds a small overall own-wage elasticity of −0.26 for the "low-skill" group of individuals aged 25 and under without a high school degree — but "for the six states (and D.C.) raising their minimums by $2.50/hour or more, they find an OWE of -1.01, while for the states raising less" the estimate is +0.46 [2].
Dube and Lindner themselves write that "further research is needed to carefully assess possible “non-linearities” from minimum wage increases that are both large and are at high levels" [2].

For teenagers — the group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and therefore the one with the most statistical power — he reports "no evidence of a publication bias" and "a minimum wage elasticity of about" −0.27 [3].
A −0.27 teenage elasticity is consistent with the −0.26 that Clemens and Strain find across all 27 of their events [2], which is a meaningful convergence from two different literatures.
Campolieti identifies teenagers as "the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers" [3], which is why the teenage estimate carries the most policy interest.
Many of these are small - the median nominal change is 3.8% - but 47 of the changes are 5% or larger" [1].

Applying an elasticity estimated on 3.8% treatments to treatments of that size is precisely the extrapolation Clemens and Strain's large-increase result says is warranted — and their finding is that at those sizes the effect is not small but very large [2].
Its headline: the median own-wage employment elasticity across 72 published studies is −0.13, which the authors characterise as "a minor impact of the minimum wage on jobs" [2].

The 15 studies of teenagers have a median own-wage elasticity of −0.17 and a mean of −0.25, and the authors concede that "the estimates for teens appear to be a bit more negative, potentially indicating more labor-labor substitution, even as the mean OWE of -0.25 still suggests any teen disemployment effect has been small" [2].

Where a single paper reports estimates for teenagers alongside estimates for a broader low-wage group, the teenage estimate is not systematically worse: Cengiz et al. find teenage elasticities of 0.36 and 0.40, and Dube and Lindner's own event studies find teenage and high-recall elasticities of 0.12 and 0.34 [2].

Their conclusion is that "there is little difference in teen and non-teen OWEs within studies; so the between-study differences in estimates uncovered above likely reflects methodological and/or sample differences" [2].

And the teenage estimates have a documented external-validity problem of their own: "the external validity of estimates based on teens is questionable, particularly since teens constitute a steadily declining share of the low-wage workforce" [2].

Across 60 combined US minimum wage events, the own-wage elasticity for restaurants is −0.03 with a standard error of 0.15; restricting to the 46 events after 1998 gives 0.15 with a standard error of 0.14 [2].
"As we can see, the event-based OWE estimates for these groups are small or positive, falling between -0.07 and 0.34" [2].

And when the authors sort their 60 events by the size of the increase — the direct test of the thesis's dosage logic — "there is no evidence of a negative association between employment estimates and the minimum wage change; the correlation coefficients are 0.17 and 0.12 for restaurants and high recall, respectively" [2].

They do not find it: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [1].
The wage distribution of Leavers is different from other workers (with more mass at lower wages) but it does not change at the time of a minimum wage increase" [1].

That this is the best Canadian mechanism test anyone has run does not make it a test of the thesis, and the honest statement of its scope is essential: their estimation window runs "from January 1997 through December 2016" [1].
What it shows is that at the treatment sizes Canada used through 2016 — a median nominal change of 3.8%, with only 47 of 157 changes at 5% or more [1] — the mechanism left no fingerprint.
(2019) and Brochu and Green (2013) as results implying small employment impacts [1].

Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for October 2026 puts the youth unemployment rate at 13.7%, up 0.7 percentage points in the month, and the youth employment rate at 54.0%, "little changed in the month and on a year-over-year basis" [5].
The deterioration is in the unemployment rate — more young people searching — rather than in a continuing collapse of the employment share [5].

Dube and Lindner test this directly and find that most event studies "do not show significantly larger medium-term effects for typical minimum wage increases observed to date", with the six-year-out employment estimates small and positive in sign [2].

First, the near-zero modern estimates are overwhelmingly American and European; Canada has a higher share of minimum wage workers and different institutions, and Campolieti's Canadian −0.27 is the evidence that the Canadian case might differ [3].
Second, Clemens and Strain's large-increase result is real: at the very largest treatment sizes, one well-known study does find an elasticity near −1 for young low-skill workers [2].

Dube and Lindner sort their 60 events by the size of the minimum wage increase and report: "However, there is no evidence of a negative association between employment estimates and the minimum wage change; the correlation coefficients are 0.17 and 0.12 for restaurants and high recall, respectively" [2].

Clemens and Strain separate the post-2013 US events by size and report an elasticity of −1.01 for low-skill workers aged 25 and under in the six states (and D.C.) that raised their floors by $2.50 an hour or more, against +0.46 in states that raised less [2].
Dube and Lindner note that "For a different group—those under 21—the two OWEs are much closer at -0.41 and -0.03" [2].
They write that "further research is needed to carefully assess possible “non-linearities” from minimum wage increases that are both large and are at high levels" [2].

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend looked for that pattern in linked Canadian Labour Force Survey mini-panels and did not find it: minimum wage increases "do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model" [1].
The wage distribution of leavers is different from other workers, but "it does not change at the time of a minimum wage increase" [1].

This is the finding most often cited as decisive against the thesis, and it is not decisive, for a reason that has to be stated plainly: the study's window "running from January 1997 through December 2016" [1] ends before the post-2017 increases begin.
It tests the mechanism at the treatment sizes Canada used up to 2016, where the median nominal change was 3.8% and only 47 of 157 changes reached 5% [1].
Two things that are often treated as decisive are not. **It does not turn on the pooled median elasticity of −0.13** [2].
Dube and Lindner confirm the method is applicable: the event-study issues are "broadly relevant also for other contexts with sub-national minimum wage variation, including Canada" [2].

It is one specific, runnable study, and the question of whether anyone has looked is answerable. **A Canadian event study on the post-2017 provincial variation.** The design is standard and Dube and Lindner confirm its applicability: the event-study methods are "broadly relevant also for other contexts with sub-national minimum wage variation, including Canada" [2].
If that study returned a teenage elasticity near −0.27 [3] with a tight standard error, the thesis would be supported and the verdict would change from Partly supported to Supported.

That conclusion is now better grounded than it was when this report began, because the OWE repository behind Dube and Lindner's 72 studies — the database from which they draw the literature — is described as "close to comprehensive for the U.S., U.K., Germany, and Canada" [2].

It is not. **A Canadian replication of the mechanism test on post-2017 data.** Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend run their separation analysis on monthly data from January 1997 through December 2016 [1] — the window ends precisely where this thesis begins.

Statistics Canada publishes the necessary monthly series by age group and province [5]. **A post-2017 Canadian event study that comes back at zero.** Given that the modern literature's central tendency is a median of −0.13 and its post-2018 US event study returns 0.15 with a standard error of 0.14 [2], this is the more likely outcome, not the less likely one. **Evidence that the no-scaling result holds in Canada.** Dube and Lindner find no negative association between the size of the increase and the employment estimate across their 60 events, with correlations of 0.17 and 0.12 [2].

If Canadian data showed the same — bigger provincial increases producing no bigger job losses — the thesis's dosage logic would be dead regardless of the sign of the average effect. **A mechanism null that survives the larger treatment sizes.** A replication of the Brochu et al. separation test on post-2017 data returning the same null at the much larger treatment sizes would be close to decisive against the stated mechanism. **If the large-increase non-linearity is real and Canada sits in it.** Clemens and Strain's −1.01 for states raising minimums by $2.50 an hour or more [2] is the one result that, if it travelled to Canada, would make the thesis not just true but important.
The best Canadian mechanism study stops in December 2016 [1].
The Canadian meta-analysis pools a literature that mostly predates the post-2017 wave [3].
The international synthesis finds the effect small and non-scaling and names large-and-high increases as the open case [2].
